articles.title: Just say no to OpenAI and Anthropic
articles.author: Micah Lee
articles.content:
I recently read End Times Fascism and the Fight for the Living World by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor. It's an excellent book and I highly recommend that everyone read it. Tech oligarchs make up an important component of the end-times-fascist coalition. One thing that stood out to me, as a software and security engineer who finds LLMs to be extremely powerful, is that the American frontier labs are run by unhinged lunatics who genuinely believe they're creating the Machine God, that they're fine with burning down the world to bring about AGI, and that they believe with religious fervor that they're the only ones smart enough to safely control it. I already kind of knew this, but this book really made it sink in.
As much as the AI hype all around us pretends that OpenAI and Anthropic are unique and special, they're not. They're not the only companies doing this work. In fact, a lot of the open weight models are just about as good as the latest ChatGPT and Claude models, including for incredibly complex tasks like vulnerability research.
Unlike models from OpenAI and Anthropic, open weight models have major advantages:
- It's possible to run them privately on your own hardware (if you can somehow get a computer with enough RAM)
- You can use a provider like Tinfoil that relies on secure enclaves to run them privately (I talk about this in a bit more detail below)
- If privacy isn't a huge concern, you can use any number of other providers, some of them quite affordable, and it's easy to switch so you're not locked into a single evil vendor
- You can still use powerful LLMs without financially supporting deranged oligarchs who gamble with life on Earth so that they can always remain in power
ChatGPT and Claude will never be private
These companies only offer closed versions of their powerful models (despite the word "open" in "OpenAI"). You pay them for chat and/or API access, and they are allowed to look at everything you do.
They offer a checkbox so you can opt out of them using your data for training, but your chat sessions still aren't private. They have access to it all. They can look at it, share it with governments or companies, or do whatever they want. It's possible, likely even, that they won't use it for training if you've opted out, at least not right now. But do you really trust that long-term? Have they done anything to make anyone believe that they respect people's data?
OpenAI and Anthropic are corporate gatekeepers
Their models have strict guardrails, as anyone who's tried to use them for anything cybersecurity-related has no doubt noticed.
Every session has a cop agent reading your transcript over your shoulder, making sure you're not using it for hacking. If it thinks you might be, the cop agent stops your session from continuing. It's very strict, and false positives happen all the time. Of course, not everyone has the cop watching them.
Some people get access to the models with looser restrictions or with none at all. OpenAI has Trusted Access for Cyber and Anthropic has the Cyber Verification Program. To gain access to more capable, less policed versions of their models, individuals and companies need to apply and be approved by OpenAI and Anthropic. A lot of US cybersecurity companies get access. Almost certainly US military contractors do too, and probably any parts of the US government that want it.
While there's some merit in restricting powerful models, handing the ultimate power to decide who gets access to them to Sam Altman and Dario Amodei – with consultation from the Trump Administration, of course – is a terrible, undemocratic idea.
I think a better approach is to simply not put yourself in a situation where you rely on ChatGPT or Claude. Instead of begging corporate overlords for privileged access, it's better to spend your time figuring out how to get models like GLM-5.3 to meet your needs. And it's not hard. These models are good, with the added benefit that they don't have a cop watching over your shoulder!
Open weight models are impressive
So far, open weight models seem to be about four months behind the fancy proprietary models from OpenAI and Anthropic.
Four months is nothing.
I'm extremely impressed right now with GLM-5.3. There's plenty of data and benchmarks out there, but my vibes-based opinion from using it is that it's basically on par with Claude Opus 5.5 for software engineering.
I'm also impressed with GLM-5.3-Flash. This is similar to Claude Opus 4.8. It's much smaller and cheaper than GLM-5.3, and still incredibly capable. It's also actually feasible for an individual person to get hardware to run it, like if you can one day get your hands on a Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM.
GLM models are made by a Chinese company called Z.ai. While the models are impressive, I don't recommend making an account directly with Z.ai or sending them any of your data. Their coding harness ZCode (their version of Claude Code) was recently caught silently uploading local source code repos and sending them back to Alibaba Cloud without consent. Also, it's safe to assume that Chinese companies will share any data you provide to them with the Chinese government.
Other open weight models from Chinese companies that are impressive include the DeepSeek, Qwen, and Kimi families of models. It's perfectly fine, safe, and secure to use these open weight models. Just don't trust the companies themselves with your chat sessions.
Another frontier AI lab worth a look is Mistral. As a French company, it's the only big player that's not Chinese or American. They just released an open weight frontier model called Mistral Large 4, aka Le Chonk. I think it's quite a bit more reasonable to trust Mistral with your data compared to the Chinese or American companies.
Private inference with Tinfoil or Maple AI
It's possible to have private AI, even without hosting it locally yourself, using secure enclaves. These aren't perfect, but I do think they provide a very meaningful difference in privacy compared to the status quo mode, which is "the provider can access everything with no restrictions."
The company that's doing the most work here is Tinfoil. If you want to learn the details, read their docs on secure enclaves and remote attestation. Another company doing this is Maple AI – although, technically, Maple uses Tinfoil for inference in the background.
Both Tinfoil and Maple are good options. Tinfoil is cheaper, but Maple is more consumer-focused.
If you want a ChatGPT-like experience, where you can talk to a chatbot, have it look stuff up for you on the internet, give it access to docs to read or do stuff with, access it in a mobile app, etc., then I'd go with Maple. There's a small free plan and a Pro plan that costs $20/month.
If you want to do real agentic coding tasks like software engineering, reverse engineering, malware analysis, CTFs or pen tests, etc., then you should use Tinfoil instead. They charge by the token for private inference, so no monthly plan. GLM-5.3 currently costs $1.80 per 1M input tokens, $0.80 per 1M cached tokens, and $5.75 per 1M output tokens. You can use significantly fewer tokens if you choose the "low" reasoning level, and it's still very impressive.
Inference without the privacy
If you don't want to pay a premium for private inference from Tinfoil or Maple, but you still want to free yourself from OpenAI and Anthropic, there are tons of less-private options that are also very cheap.
One that I've been playing with is OpenCode Go. It costs $10/month for more than $10 worth of credits. This is an inference router, which basically means your API queries do something like this: your computer -> OpenCode Go API -> the actual inference provider. This means that both OpenCode Go and whatever backend provider they're using will have access to your session data. That said, the privacy section of their docs promises which models data won't be used for training (most of them) and what the data retention is (zero days for most, including all the GLM, Qwen, Kimi, and DeepSeek models). Of course, it's just a promise. Nothing technical guarantees it.
There are plenty of other cheap options out there for non-private inference, if you just want to experiment with powerful open weight models.
How I'm using these models
I've been using both Tinfoil and OpenCode Go, configured with my current harness of choice, OpenCode. I've been mostly using GLM-5.3 on low reasoning, with great results. (Things change so quickly with the open weight models, who knows what will be best six months from now.)
I use OpenCode Go inference for completely public work, like when I'm implementing something that's already open source.
I use Tinfoil for everything else.
I've only just started working this way, but so far, I think the open weight models can easily completely replace my use of ChatGPT and Claude, at a comparable or cheaper price, with the added benefit that they're far more private and there are far fewer guardrails.
articles.summary:
Open weight artificial intelligence models offer a viable, private alternative to proprietary systems from companies like OpenAI and Anthropic, allowing users to bypass restrictive corporate gatekeeping and surveillance.

### Key Points
- Open weight models like GLM-5.3, DeepSeek, and Mistral Large 4 provide performance levels comparable to top-tier proprietary models for complex tasks like software engineering.
- Proprietary services like ChatGPT and Claude maintain strict, centralized guardrails and monitor user sessions, often restricting access to cybersecurity-related tools.
- Secure enclaves provided by services like Tinfoil and Maple AI enable private inference, preventing providers from accessing or training on sensitive user data.
- Users can avoid corporate lock-in by utilizing inference routers like OpenCode Go or hosting models locally on high-RAM hardware.
- While Chinese-developed models are technically impressive, users are advised to avoid sharing data directly with those companies due to privacy and security concerns.

### Why it Matters
Relying on closed-source AI models concentrates significant power in the hands of a few corporate entities that dictate access and monitor user activity. Transitioning to open weight models empowers individuals and developers to maintain data sovereignty while accessing high-performance tools without restrictive oversight.

articles.title: GTA 6 Leaker Promises Escalating Mayhem As Meme Coin Crashes
articles.author: Ethan Gach
articles.content:
Wanna play a game? Grand Theft Auto 6 leaker Cyberleek certainly does. Whoever is running the account is back after a long silence and won’t shut up. They’re promising an escalating series of clips depicting in-game chaos if people invest in their meme coin $Cyberleek. It hasn’t been going well.
The uniquely 2026 flavor of online grift began with the threat to leak the entire GTA 6 build Cyberleek seemingly has access to if the market cap on the cryptocurrency hit $30 million. And it seemed like there was a real shot of that happening, at least for a little while. $Cyberleek hit over $4.75 million over the weekend as the account effectively ransomed off Lucia nudes.
Cyberleek returned today, October 12, with a leak “roadmap” of the other footage they’ll allegedly release if the meme coin keeps going up:
- $5M: Mini Tank
- $9M: Tank
- $13M: Police Shootout
- $21M: Fighter Jet
- $25M: Train vs Train
- $30M: Full 200GB+ playable build
At the same time that Cyberleek was hyping these demands, however, $Cyberleek itself has been crashing. The coin’s value plummeted 50 percent in the last 24 hours, dropping the market cap to just $2.2 million. No one’s getting any GTA 6 tank battles at that rate.
All of the meme coin milestones outside of the release of the allegedly playable build seem trivial by comparison anyway. While Cyberleek has tried to claim that this entire circus is about fighting back against anti-consumer practices in the game industry–they claim the build won’t be leaked if Take-Two agrees to a disc version of GTA 6–everything surrounding it has undercut that fig leaf of a motivation.
And with the actual game’s official launch just over a month away, interest in another blurry video of GTA 6 gameplay footage showing stuff fans have already seen has been dwindling. Whether Take-Two and Rockstar are any closer to catching whoever’s behind the Cyberleek account is another question.
articles.summary:
An anonymous leaker known as Cyberleek is attempting to ransom alleged Grand Theft Auto 6 gameplay footage by tying its release to the market performance of a meme coin.

### Key Points
- The leaker claims to possess a 200GB playable build of Grand Theft Auto 6 and various gameplay clips.
- Access to the alleged footage is contingent on the $Cyberleek cryptocurrency reaching specific market capitalization milestones up to $30 million.
- The $Cyberleek token value dropped 50% in 24 hours, currently holding a market cap of approximately $2.2 million.
- The account operator claims the scheme protests anti-consumer practices, specifically demanding a physical disc version of the game from publisher Take-Two.
- Official release of Grand Theft Auto 6 is scheduled for late 2025, with no confirmation regarding the authenticity of the leaked materials.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights the growing trend of using high-profile intellectual property leaks to manipulate volatile cryptocurrency markets. It underscores the ongoing security challenges faced by major game publishers like Rockstar Games as they approach highly anticipated product launches.

articles.title: Russia Was Not Ready For the Data Center War It Started With Ukraine
articles.author: BeauHD
articles.content:
An anonymous reader quotes a report from Ars Technica: When Russia began attacking Ukrainian data centers and telecommunication infrastructure, it apparently failed to prepare for possible retaliation. Now Russia's digital services are facing widespread outages after Ukrainian drone strikes knocked out three of the largest data centers owned by Russian tech giant Yandex within several days. Pro-Kremlin bloggers are warning that Russia's centralized digital economy could collapse because the country is not prepared for the "data center war" it started, according to posts translated by the pseudonymous independent researcher ChrisO_wiki. The Russian commentators also suggested that Ukraine's decentralized digital services could prove more resilient than Russia's system if the countries continue trading such blows.
Russia initially launched a drone strike campaign targeting Ukrainian data centers and mobile phone networks in late September. The attacks temporarily disrupted Internet and cell phone service for up to 100,000 households in the Ukrainian capital of Kyiv and came as part of a broader long-range strike campaign that has involved Russian missiles and jet-powered drones hitting Ukraine's power grid infrastructure, transportation hubs, and even residential apartment building blocks. But Ukraine soon began striking back at data centers owned by the Russian company Yandex, also known as "Russia's Google," in what Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has described as a "symmetrical response."
[...] More importantly for Russian society, the damage to Yandex's data centers has reportedly caused interruptions or outages to popular Russian payment apps and digital banking services, email, e-commerce platforms, video streaming services, ride-hailing and food delivery apps, and navigation and map services. Yandex's search engine also accounts for about 70 percent of the market share in Russia. The disruptions are even more widespread, because the data center damage also impacts Yandex's cloud computing service, which counts some of Russia's largest companies as customers, according to The Moscow Times, an independent newspaper. These include large grocery and fast-food chains as well as a household appliance retailer.
articles.summary:
Ukrainian drone strikes against three major Yandex data centers have triggered widespread digital service outages across Russia, highlighting the vulnerability of the nation's centralized technological infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Ukrainian forces targeted three Yandex data centers in a retaliatory campaign following Russian strikes on Ukrainian telecommunications and power infrastructure.
- The outages have disrupted essential Russian services, including digital banking, payment apps, e-commerce, ride-hailing, and navigation platforms.
- Yandex, often described as "Russia's Google," holds approximately 70 percent of the domestic search market and provides critical cloud computing services to major corporations.
- Pro-Kremlin commentators have expressed concerns that Russia’s centralized digital economy is ill-equipped to withstand a sustained "data center war."
- Independent reports suggest that Ukraine’s decentralized digital architecture may offer greater resilience against similar long-range strike campaigns.

### Why it Matters
The disruption of Yandex services demonstrates the significant risks posed to modern economies when centralized digital infrastructure becomes a primary target in military conflicts. This escalation suggests that critical civilian technology platforms are increasingly vulnerable to retaliatory strikes, potentially destabilizing daily commerce and essential public services.

articles.title: How Apple can win the smart home
articles.author: Jennifer Pattison Tuohy
articles.content:
This week, Apple is hosting its first-ever dedicated smart home event. While the company hasn’t shared details about what it will reveal at the “Welcome Home experience” in New York City on Tuesday, October 13th, it doesn’t take an army of internet sleuths to deduce we’ll get news about Apple Home — specifically, new hardware. Apple finally seems to be taking the smart home seriously.
How Apple can win the smart home
New hardware could put Apple back in the race, but software will determine whether it wins.
According to Bloomberg, Apple will release a smart home display alongside a refreshed HomePod Mini and Apple TV. The display, which MacRumors reports may be called HomeView, is arguably Apple’s first dedicated Apple Home hardware since it launched the HomeKit platform in 2014. As exciting as this is (and I’ll be there in person to check it out), the real shift will be bringing Siri AI and Apple Intelligence into the home. Apple is years behind Google and Amazon in smart-home hardware, but success in the home depends far more on software. That’s where Apple could leapfrog the competition.
New home hardware is long overdue. Apple announced the HomePod Mini on October 13th, 2020, six years to the day from this week’s event, and the newest Apple TV 4K is now four years old. And those aren’t dedicated smart home devices; they’re more content-consumption gadgets with a side of home automation. The new smart display is reportedly designed to be the heart of Apple Home, marking a complete reboot of the ecosystem, and Apple Home users have wanted it for years.
The smart display category has a bumpy history. Amazon and Google have launched several generations of these voice- and touchscreen-controlled smart speakers that can control smart home gadgets like lights and locks, pull up doorbell camera feeds, and make video calls. But the category has seen very little innovation, and its best use case has been serving as a digital photo frame.
Based on leaks, Apple’s product doesn’t sound that different from what’s come before. According to Bloomberg, it will have a 6-inch square display on a speaker base or as a wall-mounted option, facial recognition to show your personal messages and calendar, a minimalist touchscreen interface to control locks and thermostats, and FaceTime and intercom calls. Nothing groundbreaking, except the rumored price — $350, ouch. The difference has to be in the software and the smart assistant that powers it.
Bloomberg reports the smart display will launch with a brand-new homeOS built around Siri AI. Generative AI has breathed new life into the smart home voice assistant by both making it easier to talk to and expanding its capabilities. Until now, Apple’s new Siri AI has been MIA from its HomePods and Apple TV; when you talk to those, the old Siri responds in its basic, functional way.
Apple is the last of the big three to bring generative AI to its home assistant. Amazon and Google launched theirs last year, but Alexa Plus is only just starting to get it right, and Google’s Gemini for Home, an underpowered version of Gemini, is a confusing mess of capabilities. Now it’s Apple’s turn, and if the company can successfully merge its superpowered personal assistant on your iPhone with a superpowered assistant for your home, it may have a hit on its hands.
That’s a very big if. So far, every company has hit significant roadblocks bringing a smarter assistant to the home. Apple announced Apple Intelligence in 2024, but Siri AI only arrived last month; a version of Alexa Plus was announced in 2023 but didn’t launch until 2025; Gemini for Home is still in an early access program and split into a weird hybrid model where its more capable version, Gemini Live, is restricted from interacting with the home.
These cautious approaches are down to the fact that the home is a big, complicated, messy, multi-user environment that is hard to control. An agentic AI getting something wrong could have consequences far greater than accidentally sending an email. Smart home systems are connected to critical infrastructure like HVAC, locks, and security systems. Every home is different, with unique needs — there is no single plug-and-play solution.
Progress has been made toward solving one of the smart home’s biggest challenges: interoperability, with open standards like Matter and Thread promising to make setting up and using a smart home easier. But these are protocols, not software. It’s the platforms that have to make the smart home work. Here is where Apple may have the edge.
Four years ago, after helping found Matter, Apple rebuilt HomeKit’s underlying architecture and revamped the Home app, laying a strong foundation. That move also let Apple Home work with more devices from more manufacturers (previously, it was limited to those willing to go through the often arduous HomeKit approval process).
However, a smart home isn’t just about the devices you put in it. It’s about making them work together. That’s where Siri AI and Apple Intelligence could play a major role. While Apple used Gemini models to build Siri AI, Google itself has struggled to deliver a compelling experience in the home. So Apple’s opportunity lies in execution. Its more curated approach to third-party hardware has held it back, but it also means Apple arrives at this crucial moment with less technical debt and a cleaner foundation for building an AI-powered smart home.
This will be the next level for the smart home; with reliable data and context, your home could know who’s in it, where they are, and what they need, and, combined with knowing the status of every device, become proactive. For example, it could alert you that the oven is on and no one is home, suggest turning off the AC when a window is left open, and route messages and notifications to the room you’re in.
A smart home isn’t just about the devices you put in it. It’s about making them work together
This is still a distant promise, however. Today, Apple Home has significant limitations: it doesn’t support every type of home device (no fridges, washing machines, or EV chargers); it can’t control every feature of many device types; and its automations are limited compared to the competition (notably lacking conditional programming options inside the app). All this makes the Home app very easy to use, but extremely underpowered.
With Siri AI, Apple could unlock many of those capabilities via voice instead of building complicated menu interfaces. You could just tell Siri what you want your smart home to do. Alexa Plus offers this with the ability to create routines using your voice; Gemini for Home lets you use natural language in its Home app chatbot to set up automations; and many smart home companies are adopting AI in their apps to cut through UI complexity and make devices and features easier to use.
A big question remains: do people really want a smart home? Many of us have spent years frustrated with systems that hold so much promise but routinely fail to deliver, leaving us spending weekends troubleshooting why the garage door won’t open. The truly dedicated have turned to Home Assistant, a powerful platform that can do almost anything you want, if you’re willing to do the work. But for most people, beyond a few solutions to specific problems, the smart home just isn’t worth it.
Apple can’t make everything for the smart home, but it can make sure that everything works with its platform.
To win in the smart home and bring the category mainstream, Apple needs more than just great hardware; it needs a superior software experience that makes the smart home easy to use. It needs to integrate seamlessly with third-party devices and deliver a consistent, reliable experience, relying on local control wherever possible and making sure products just work.
Apple is reportedly partnering with LG and others to develop products for an “Apple Home Collection” that will add a layer of Apple polish to the smart home experience. While this might sound like going back to the walled garden of the HomeKit days, Matter ensures interoperability with other platforms. Apple can’t make everything for the smart home, but it can make sure that everything works with its platform.
Most crucially, Apple will need to double down on its commitment to privacy and data security, especially as it opens the home to Apple Intelligence’s cloud-based capabilities. If Apple can deliver on all of this, its highly anticipated smart home display might justify its price. But the real test will be whether Siri can make the smart home live up to its promise.
articles.summary:
Apple is hosting a dedicated smart home event in New York City on October 13th, where it is expected to unveil a new AI-powered smart display device.

### Key Points
- Apple is reportedly launching a 6-inch smart display, potentially named HomeView, featuring a touchscreen, facial recognition, and FaceTime capabilities.
- The new hardware is expected to run on a brand-new homeOS integrated with Siri AI and Apple Intelligence.
- The device is rumored to carry a $350 price point and will serve as a central hub for the Apple Home ecosystem.
- Apple is reportedly partnering with manufacturers like LG to develop a curated "Apple Home Collection" of compatible smart devices.
- The company aims to address long-standing smart home challenges by leveraging the Matter and Thread interoperability standards.

### Why it Matters
This event marks Apple’s most significant attempt to compete with Amazon and Google in the smart home market by shifting focus from simple hardware to AI-driven automation. If successful, the integration of Apple Intelligence could transform the smart home from a collection of disconnected gadgets into a proactive, user-aware ecosystem.

articles.title: Anthropic is making a $100 million bet on deployed AI engineers, and it seeks 5 key attributes
articles.author: Stephen Council
articles.content:
Forward-deployed engineers are all the rage in AI, and Anthropic is going to other companies to train up top talent.
The AI company announced a $100 million investment into an FDE training initiative earlier this month. It's a quasi-fellowship that engineers from other firms have already begun applying for. They'll attend four-day on-site intensives and then complete 12-week "residencies" working with Anthropic's Claude tools at their own companies. The company says it hopes to train 10,000 people through the program by the end of 2027.
As Anthropic approaches its gigantic initial public offering, it's using the new training model to get more of the corporate world used to AI — and ramp up Claude spending. Job postings for FDEs have boomed over the last couple of years, as more companies buy software from AI firms and need help deploying it.
Two Anthropic executives leading the push told Business Insider that their customers see AI's advances, notice competitors grabbing market share, and feel pressure to change their own work.
"Everybody understands the model capability is expanding extremely fast," said Shambhavi Shambhavi, Anthropic's head of go-to-market strategy and operations for partnerships. "So, what can be done with the technology is greatly appreciated by the customers."
Enter the FDE — which Anthropic calls "Frontier Deployed Engineers," rather than the standard "forward-deployed engineer" title that Palantir helped popularize. Both roles essentially mean someone with deep technical expertise in AI and the mandate to create new modes of work at a company.
Shambhavi and Steve Corfield, Anthropic's head of global business development and partnerships, broke down the FDE role as they see it and how Anthropic hopes to set a "gold standard" with its new skills push.
Anthropic execs say FDEs are curious
Shambhavi said that the best FDEs have four main attributes. They are familiar with agentic AI systems. They're good problem-solvers. They're excellent communicators. And they're experienced, skilled engineers.
Corfield tacked on a point he thinks helps Anthropic thrive: "You've got to be super, super curious. If you walk around this organization, everybody talks about curiosity."
Communication is particularly important, Shambhavi said. She said that as companies try to overhaul entire workflows and approach agentic AI holistically, someone who can navigate the interpersonal dynamics goes a long way.
"Our own Frontier Deployed Engineers work with these kinds of problems day in and day out," Shambhavi said. "And so we kind of applied the mindset of, we need to take this skill and bring it to our customers and partners and to the top engineers in those organizations, so that they can derive the benefits from Claude."
Anthropic wants to set the 'gold standard' for AI skills
Engineers who can expand their teams' use of AI have become a hot commodity in Silicon Valley. Salesforce, a major Anthropic partner, announced a plan in May to recruit 1,000 early-career workers into "AI builder" roles. Anthropic's program, in Corfield's view, goes a step above other industry attempts to recruit and train FDEs. Combined with other company initiatives to teach people AI, he hopes Anthropic will set "the gold standard for AI skilling."
The first cohorts have begun in New York and San Francisco, including engineers from Accenture, Bain, Novo Nordisk, and other organizations.
Companies nominate engineers for the training, and Anthropic interviews candidates. If they're accepted, they work for the four-day residency on a "simulated environment," an agentic system that they have to learn how to build and deploy. Then they take a practical test, before returning to their companies while staying in touch with Anthropic mentors for 12 more weeks.
Anthropic is still building its assessments throughout the program. Shambhavi said they'll focus on "what does a great FDE look like" — articulation, problem solving, coding skills.
Corfield said corporate customers wanted a program like this to help them figure out how to deploy Claude more effectively, and the holdup isn't motivation.
"This is a skills gap problem, and that creates a market problem," he said.
"What we're trying to do is fill that gap," he added.

articles.summary:
Anthropic has launched a $100 million training initiative to certify 10,000 "Frontier Deployed Engineers" by 2027, aiming to accelerate corporate adoption of its Claude AI software tools.

### Key Points
- Anthropic’s program includes four-day on-site intensives followed by 12-week residencies where engineers implement Claude within their own organizations.
- The initiative targets a goal of training 10,000 professionals by the end of 2027 to address the growing industry-wide AI skills gap.
- Early participants include engineers from major firms such as Accenture, Bain, and Novo Nordisk, with cohorts currently operating in New York and San Francisco.
- The curriculum focuses on agentic AI systems, requiring candidates to pass practical tests on building and deploying AI in simulated environments.
- Anthropic aims to establish a "gold standard" for AI deployment expertise to differentiate its technology and increase enterprise spending on its platform.

### Why it Matters
This initiative addresses a critical bottleneck in the AI market where companies possess the desire to innovate but lack the technical talent to deploy complex agentic systems. By standardizing the role of the Frontier Deployed Engineer, Anthropic is effectively creating a proprietary ecosystem that encourages long-term reliance on its Claude models.

articles.title: Edifier’s $52 gaming soundbar lets you ditch your headset without losing voice chat
articles.author: Gaurav Sood
articles.content:
Gaming soundbars became popular in the 2017s, but the trend faded; in the last couple of years, this category of audio accessories has seen renewed interest. Razer kicked off the new wave, with several mainstream brands and some offbeat makers releasing their own versions. Creative recently launched their B3 soundbar for gamers at a very affordable price, and now Edifier is upping the ante with an even sweeter deal.
The China-based audio accessories maker, known for high-end bookshelf speakers, has come up with a very cool-looking soundbar for gamers. Dubbed the Hecate G2000 Bar, the desktop audio boomer is all set to be available from 16 October onwards for a price tag of 349 yuan ($52), which is an introductory price slashed from the normal price of 387 yuan ($58).
The G2000 Bar combines a compact footprint with an angular, mecha-inspired design intended to fit into a gaming setup without taking up much desk space. It will be available in black and white, with a built-in five-degree upward tilt that directs sound toward the listener rather than across the desktop. Five interchangeable themed stickers let users customize the front panel, while 12 RGB lighting effects, including rainbow and flowing-light patterns, add some visual flair. Lighting can be adjusted via the Edifier Connect mobile app or Hecate PC software.
Under the hood, the soundbar uses two 56mm full-range drivers with copper-clad aluminum wire voice coils, paired with two 60mm passive radiators. The arrangement is designed to deliver fuller audio and reinforce low frequencies without requiring a separate subwoofer. Output is rated at 3W per channel, or 6W in total, with peak power reaching 12W. The stated frequency response spans 67Hz to 20kHz.
For gaming, the G2000 Bar supports THX 7.1.4 spatial audio processing, which aims to create a more immersive, surround-like listening experience from a desktop soundbar. Six dedicated audio presets cater to different gaming genres, including first-person shooters, role-playing games, and racing titles. These modes give players a way to tailor the sound to different types of gameplay without manually adjusting equalizer settings.
The other notable addition is a detachable microphone mounted on top. It uses AEC 2.0 acoustic echo cancellation, a dedicated digital signal processor, and AI-assisted noise reduction to limit background sounds and reduce audio feedback from the speakers. This could make voice chat more convenient for players who prefer open speakers to a gaming headset, although performance will depend on the surrounding environment.
Connectivity includes Bluetooth 6.0 and USB sound-card input, allowing the soundbar to work with compatible PCs, laptops, mobile devices, and consoles. An independent 9V DC power adapter supplies power, while physical controls on the top metallic panel provide access to volume adjustment, microphone muting, and audio-mode switching.

articles.title: Galaxy S27 Ultra might take eye strain seriously amid rumors of DC dimming
articles.author: nickodiaz@sbcglobal.net (Nickolas Diaz) , Nickolas Diaz
articles.content:
What you need to know
- A rumor claims that Samsung may introduce DC dimming to the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra.
- The company is reportedly working with "various safety firms" to understand how to reduce eye strain on its future Galaxy phones.
- Nicholas Sutrich dove deep into PWM dimming and DC dimming once upon a time, and his feelings side with the latter that's more human-friendly.
Amongst all of the Galaxy S27 series rumors, this one deserves some attention. Rumors claim Samsung might start taking eye strain reduction seriously.
Rumors about this stem from tipster Walle on X, who states Samsung is looking to integrate new eye strain reduction tech into the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra (via Android Headlines). The post claims both devices could benefit from DC dimming. It's been reported that Samsung is allegedly beginning to "collaborate" with "various safety firms to understand how to lessen eye strain problems."
Walle adds that these improvements (and more) will arrive for Samsung's Eye Comfort Shield. Currently, you can find this option in your Galaxy device's Display settings. When toggled, your device will limit its blue light by using warmer colors. Moreover, it will automatically adjust your screen's colors based on the time (if set to automatic).
On the surface, this rumor sounds like a win for people who suffer from headaches and eye strain when using their phones for extended periods. But there's more to know, considering Samsung's Galaxy phones already use PWM dimming.
PWM or DC dimming?
We love using our phones. What hurts is having to stop. Whether you're reading or watching a show or playing a game, the last thing you want is to feel a horrendous headache. If we can have phones that reduce that risk for those prone to it, that'd make the user experience that much better. We're paying hundreds and even thousands for these phones. Why are side effects included?
My former colleague Nicholas Sutrich was the person to go to whenever PWM dimming was brought. But what is it? In Sutrich's own words, "...modern smartphone displays don't dim like they used to, or even like a traditional lightbulb. Instead, they often rapidly turn on and off to fool your eyes into seeing a dimmer image."
This is Pulse Width Modulation (PWM dimming). This is a piece of technology most commonly used in OLED and AMOLED. Sutrich said, "Companies use PWM dimming because OLEDs can exhibit visual problems when trying to dim them like a traditional light source." However, the most clever ones realize they could "just turn it on and off very rapidly, and the human brain does the rest."
While PWM dimming is fine, Sutrich felt that DC dimming is better. DC-like dimming on OnePlus phones activates when your brightness is over 25%. If it dips below this line, the phone reverts to the crazy flickering of PWM dimming. Why? Sutrich said, "This is because, unlike PWM dimming, DC-like dimming never turns the entire display off when it refreshes. There's just a small brightness drop as each pixel is refreshed."

Hopefully we see this change for the Galaxy S27 Pro and S27 Ultra, but who knows.
Nickolas is always excited about tech and getting his hands on it. Writing for him can vary from delivering the latest tech story to scribbling in his journal. When Nickolas isn't hitting a story, he's often grinding away at a game or chilling with a book in his hand.

articles.title: Hackers defrost fridges at hundreds of French supermarkets, Bloomberg says
articles.author: Darius Popa
articles.content:
Hackers broke into the refrigeration systems of hundreds of French supermarkets on Sunday night. Stores had to throw out meat, frozen goods and vegetables.
About 150 Intermarché stores were hit, a spokesman for owner Groupement Mousquetaires told Bloomberg. The attackers set the cooling systems to defrost.
Fridges and freezers heated to 50°C for around six hours, the spokesman said.
Super U and Leclerc also hit
Coopérative U was also targeted, chief executive Dominique Schelcher said on X. Fewer than 100 of its stores were affected, Agence France-Presse reported.
Some Leclerc stores were hit too, French broadcaster BFM reported. Leclerc did not immediately respond to Bloomberg’s request for comment.
A known weak spot
Mousquetaires said the systems were managed by Danfoss, the Danish refrigeration group. It said it was up to the supplier to file a complaint with the authorities.
In August, Claroty’s Team82 researchers flagged flaws in Danfoss controllers used in supermarkets and cold stores. They found a hidden login, based on a daily code, that could give an attacker admin access.
Team82 said Danfoss had released a firmware fix. It also found thousands of the controllers reachable from the internet.
It is not yet known whether those flaws were used on Sunday. Neither the retailers nor Danfoss have said how the attackers got in.
The incident adds to a run of attacks that halt operations rather than steal data. The JLR hack and the Boston Scientific breach both disrupted physical production and shipping.

articles.summary:
Hackers compromised refrigeration systems at hundreds of French supermarkets, including Intermarché and Super U locations, forcing stores to discard large quantities of perishable food after forced defrosting.

### Key Points
- Attackers remotely set refrigeration units to 50°C for six hours, causing widespread spoilage of meat, frozen goods, and vegetables.
- Approximately 150 Intermarché stores and nearly 100 Coopérative U locations were confirmed as targets, with additional reports involving Leclerc stores.
- The affected cooling systems are managed by the Danish supplier Danfoss, which previously released firmware fixes for security vulnerabilities identified by researchers in August.
- Cybersecurity firm Claroty’s Team82 previously warned that thousands of Danfoss controllers remained reachable via the internet with potential administrative access flaws.
- Retailers and Danfoss have not yet confirmed the specific method used to breach the systems or whether the known vulnerabilities were exploited.

### Why it Matters
This incident highlights a growing trend of cyberattacks that prioritize physical operational disruption over traditional data theft. As critical infrastructure becomes increasingly connected, these breaches pose significant financial risks to retailers and threaten the stability of food supply chains.

articles.title: AI minister warns 'likely' UK's cyber defences will be breached
articles.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
articles.content:
- Published
The UK's AI minister has warned it is "likely, if not inevitable" the country's cyber defences will at some point be breached.
Speaking at a press conference, Kanishka Narayan pointed to an incident of a rogue OpenAI agent hacking an Australian government website in June.
He said while no medical records are known to have been accessed in the attack, the incident should still "concern us".
Narayan said the government plans to put advanced AI to work to combat the threat, as he set out how the government plans to prepare for any serious future incidents.
The minister said the move would build on two existing pilots which have helped identify and fix over 1,000 vulnerabilities across government systems.
He said his message to the largest companies behind the world's most powerful AI systems was: "Listen when your scientists warn of serious dangers. Investigate unexpected behaviour. And if you cannot adequately control the risks, do not release the system."
In his speech, Narayan also confirmed scientists at the UK's AI watchdog, the AI Security Institute (AISI), were conducting "rigorous evaluations" of the latest generation of advanced AI models to "identify risks early" and "to test robust safeguards to help keep people safe".
AI testing
AISI began evaluating risks of the latest frontier AI models, prior to their public release, shortly after it was established in November 2023.
But it was reported in September, external that the White House had asked some leading US labs not to share their models with the research organisation until its own tests were completed.
The move was viewed at the time as a blow to AISI - which has been championed by the UK government and its partners for advancing open, constructive and collaborative AI testing.
Microsoft president Brad Smith recently told the BBC the institute had helped cement the UK as the country best-placed to drive forward global regulation.
On Monday, Narayan said that in the last few weeks, the government had worked with the US "to retain access for Britain's AISI to the most powerful AI models before they are released".
He also said the UK would also look into creating stronger protections through the Cyber Security and Resilience bill, particularly at how serious AI incidents can be identified and reported.
Nuala Polo, UK Public Policy Lead at the Ada Lovelace Institute, said the announcement committed the government to "very little".
"Stronger protections will be 'considered', strengthening the Cyber Bill 'explored' and near-miss reporting 'looked at', with the detail to come later," she said.
"There is no new regulatory power, no timetable and no obligation on AI developers."
Regulation
The announcement follows a series of incidents involving AI agents across major firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic acting outside human control and hacking into external systems.
On 9 September, Evan Hubinger, a top safety researcher at Anthropic, warned in a post on X that AI is advancing so quickly he believed there is a greater than 10% chance it "could kill all humans" within the next decade.
The bosses of the US-based AI giants such as Anthropic, OpenAI and Google DeepMind have all backed the idea of an AI development slowdown.
However, there are currently no global safety rules in place to regulate the companies and their technology. President Trump has called for the sector to regulate itself so that US firms do not lose out to Chinese rivals.
Speaking to the BBC following the announcement, Narayan said the UK needed "to be confident... as a country" when questioned as to how the government can make foreign AI firms abide by UK rules.
"We have the capability, we have the trust, and we have a government that is right on the side of the British public in making sure we don't just have laws but the ability to enforce those laws," he said.
"What we are focused on is delivering the right outcome for the British public, where the law was the answer."
On the question of whether the UK should have its own sovereign AI frontier model, the minister said he was "focused" on securing British sovereignty, which meant "placing the right set of investments".
"It's British chips being made here. It's British models outside of just language, looking at things like drug discovery, materials discovery, computer vision and its areas of adoption, including AI, security and cyber-security," he said.
articles.summary:
UK AI Minister Kanishka Narayan warned that cyber breaches are inevitable and announced plans to utilize advanced AI to strengthen national security against emerging technological threats.

### Key Points
- Minister Kanishka Narayan stated that cyberattacks on UK government systems are likely, citing a recent incident where a rogue OpenAI agent hacked an Australian government website.
- The UK government plans to expand the use of AI to identify and patch vulnerabilities, building on two pilot programs that already fixed over 1,000 security flaws.
- The UK’s AI Security Institute (AISI) is conducting rigorous pre-release evaluations of frontier AI models to identify risks and establish robust safety safeguards.
- The government recently secured an agreement with the US to maintain AISI access to the most powerful AI models before they are released to the public.
- New protections are being considered under the upcoming Cyber Security and Resilience bill to improve the identification and reporting of serious AI-related incidents.

### Why it Matters
This announcement highlights the growing tension between rapid AI development and the urgent need for national cybersecurity infrastructure. By pushing for stricter oversight and international collaboration, the UK aims to mitigate risks posed by autonomous AI agents while attempting to maintain a competitive edge in global technology regulation.

articles.title: ⚡ Weekly Recap: Helpdesk 0-Days, Rogue Certs, ShinyHunters Arrest, AI-Fooling Malware and More

articles.content:
Some meetings last longer than it took attackers to jump on a newly disclosed security flaw this week. Within hours, they were already testing it. That's not much time to read the warning, let alone do something about it.
But speed is only part of the problem. A secure connection didn't always mean a safe destination. People offering to fix a ransomware mess had questions to answer themselves. Malware got better at hiding its tracks. And some systems turned out to be easier to break into than anyone would like to admit. The odd part is how normal much of it looked until someone checked closer.
There's more going on here than a few bad bugs and clever attacks. Some of the smaller stories are just as telling. This week's full recap is worth a read, especially the bits that didn't make the big headlines.
⚡ Threat of the Week
Atlassian Flaw Exploited in the Wild — Threat actors have begun to exploit a newly disclosed critical security flaw impacting Atlassian Data Center products that could allow access to sensitive files under certain conditions. The arbitrary file access flaw, tracked as CVE-2026-21589 (CVSS score: 9.3) affects multiple products, including Bitbucket Data Center, Confluence Data Center, Jira Service Management Data Center, Jira Software Data Center, Bamboo Data Center, Crowd Data Center, Crucible, and Fisheye. The exploitation activity targeting its honeypot network is said to have begun two hours after watchTowr released additional technical details of the vulnerability.

🔔 Top News
- Ransomware Recovery CEO Charged for Secretly Paying Hackers — Zohar Pinhasi, the owner of Florida-based ransomware recovery firm MonsterCloud, was hit with wire fraud charges for allegedly falsely claiming he could help victims restore data without paying ransoms. Instead, prosecutors said Pinhasi simply paid ransoms and charged victims a fee that was significantly higher than the original ransom demand. MonsterCloud was also highlighted in a 2019 ProPublica investigation on companies defrauding ransomware victims by paying ransoms and charging exorbitant fees.
- New DarkSword Variant Detected — A previously unseen variant of the DarkSword iOS exploit kit called P7 DarkSword has been updated to support on-device keychain and crypto-wallet theft, and facilitate two-way C2 communication with the attacker's infrastructure. The new variant is much better at hiding itself and cleaning up its behavior, rendering previous indicators of compromise (IOCs) ineffective. The changes indicate substantial work by the operators rather than simple modifications. The most important change is that it can extract Keychain data directly on the iPhone before sending it to the attackers, as opposed to copying the entire Keychain database for processing remotely. Evidence indicates that the exploit kit is distributed via malicious ads as part of watering hole attacks.
- UAC-0099 Continues to Update MATCHBOIL Malware — The Russia-aligned threat actor known as UAC-0099 is actively refining a malware downloader called MATCHBOIL, suggesting it intends to use the tool in future attacks. Over the past year, MATCHBOIL has evolved from a dropper that essentially executed once, contacted its C2 server, and downloaded and installed a next-stage payload, into one that's run every two minutes. The change allows it to repeatedly contact its control server and fetch new or updated payloads.
- FBI Disrupts Hacking Tools and Domains Linked to Flax Typhoon — The U.S. Federal Bureau of Investigation (FBI) and Department of Justice (DoJ) announced the disruption of malicious tools used by a China-linked advanced persistent threat group known as Flax Typhoon. While Microscan was used to conduct reconnaissance and computer vulnerability scanning, FishHub allegedly enabled the exploitation of computer networks through spear-phishing attacks and the deployment of follow-on payloads. CISA's acting executive assistant director for cybersecurity, Chris Butera, said Chinese government hackers "continue to position themselves within critical infrastructure networks, including operational technology (OT) systems, with the aim of disrupting critical functions at a future time of their choosing." Integrity Technology is best known in China for developing the country's cyber ranges and has publicly touted its extensive government funding in the past. Natto Thoughts research said the company was founded in 2010 by Cai Jingjing, a legendary hacker in China.
- Another ShinyHunters Arrest Made — FBI said it made a third arrest in connection with the ShinyHunters group, as the net closes around the notorious cybercrime group. "Our agents in the field have arrested another suspected co-conspirator of the ShinyHunters group – the group believed to be responsible for the recent FBIjobs.gov incident, which occurred on a platform managed by a third-party vendor," FBI director Kash Patel said. Although the identity of the individual was not disclosed, court documents, POLITICO, and independent security journalist Brian Krebs said it was Edward Dubrovsky, a 54-year-old cybersecurity executive and investor based in Toronto. Dubrovsky has been charged with conspiracy to threaten to impair the confidentiality of information with the intent to extort money, and interference with commerce by threats. It is the third publicly announced arrest since news of the breach came out in late September 2026. In a Telegram post, the group said, "We will not remain active on Telegram for much longer, as several of our members have reportedly been arrested by the FBI."
- Attackers Hijack Three ccTLDs to Obtain Google Certificates — Google said unknown threat actors obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates for several Google domains and hijacked domains in the country-code top-level domains (ccTLDs) for Ghana (.gh), American Samoa (.as), and Sierra Leone (.sl) after compromising third-party operators and modifying authoritative DNS records. "During these hijacks, attackers modified authoritative DNS records and obtained unauthorized HTTPS certificates covering several Google domains, as well as domains belonging to other organizations," Google said. "Following our initial mitigation, Certificate Transparency (CT) log data revealed additional organizations, including several leading global brands and widely used online services, believed to have been impacted by the same attacks." Chrome blocked the unauthorized certificates through CRLSets.
- GoBalance Flaw Can Be Used to Hijack TOR .onion Sites — A vulnerability in GoBalance, a load-balancing tool used by many darknet sites, can be abused to recover a site's master signing scalar from its publicly available data, ultimately enabling site takeover and redirection. "Between 5 and 7 October, both onion addresses of Dread, a prominent darknet forum, were taken over and redirected to a rival platform, Conclave," Searchlight Cyber said. "Several marketplaces using the same software were also affected. Dread's operators initially attributed the incident to an accidental key leak; the evidence set out below indicates that the GoBalance flaw was the more likely cause, at least for the second address."
️🔥 Trending CVEs
Bugs drop weekly, and the gap between a patch and an exploit is shrinking fast. These are the heavy hitters for the week: high-severity, widely used, or already being poked at in the wild.
Check the list, patch what you have, and hit the ones marked urgent first — CVE-2026-86360, CVE-2026-86361, CVE-2026-86362 (Dell System Update), CVE-2026-21589 (Atlassian), CVE-2026-93355 (LiteLLM), CVE-2026-106382, CVE-2026-106197, CVE-2026-106358, CVE-2026-106347 (Google Chrome), CVE-2026-102255 (SonicWall SMA 1000), CVE-2026-105192 (LMCache), CVE-2026-102406, CVE-2026-103008, CVE-2026-102404, CVE-2026-102413 (Elasticsearch), CVE-2026-104711, CVE-2026-104712, CVE-2026-104713, CVE-2026-104714 (Apache Struts), CVE-2026-91140 (Progress DataDirect), CVE-2025-64393, CVE-2026-58069 (Veeam Backup & Replication), CVE-2026-32740 (Next.js), CVE-2026-18397 (Thales SConnect), CVE-2026-84388 (Fortinet FortiPAM Chrome extension), CVE-2026-76464, CVE-2026-20328, CVE-2026-76454, CVEs, CVE-2026-76482, CVE-2026-76480, CVE-2026-76483, CVE-2026-76455, CVE-2026-76459, CVE-2026-76471, CVE-2026-76465, CVE-2026-76485, CVE-2026-76486, CVE-2026-76501, CVE-2026-76498, CVE-2026-76499, CVE-2026-76500 (Cisco), CVE-2026-76281, CVE-2026-76282, CVE-2026-76284, CVE-2026-76268 (Splunk), CVE-2026-85097 (Bricksforge WordPress plugin), CVE-2026-93836 (WPC Product Bundles for WooCommerce WordPress plugin), CVE-2026-94504 (Ninja Forms WordPress plugin), CVE-2026-105133, CVE-2026-105134 (AhsayCBS), CVE-2026-96940 (Microsoft Exchange Server), CVE-2026-63277 (LibreOffice), CVE-2026-59265 (Apache OpenOffice), and multiple vulnerabilities in WordPress.
🎥 Cybersecurity Webinars

Can Your Identity Security Keep Up? → AI-powered attacks can now move from reconnaissance to privilege escalation faster than traditional security teams can investigate and respond. This webinar explains why identity is becoming the critical real-time control layer—and how runtime identity security can help organizations detect risky access, enforce decisions across cloud, SaaS, on-prem, and AI environments, and stop machine-speed attacks before they turn into breaches.

This webinar breaks down how shadow AI creates insider risk and shows how to govern AI access, reduce exposure, and enable safer adoption without slowing the business.
📰 Around the Cyber World
- The India-nexus adversary known as Dropping Elephant (aka Patchwork) has been observed targeting government, defense, naval, aerospace/UAV, academic, and other strategically significant sectors across Pakistan, Sri Lanka, China, and South Korea. "The group continues to use spear-phishing campaigns with malicious LNK attachments to deliver PowerShell-based malware, DLL sideloading payloads, and in-memory RAT," Arctic Wolf said.
- Bitter, another threat actor assessed to be operating with interests aligned to India, targeted a European embassy in Asia in June 2026 with a spear-phishing email bearing a FIFA World Cup-themed lure to deliver BDarkRAT. "The attackers compromised a legitimate mailbox belonging to a diplomatic account from an African country to send the malicious message," Trellix said. "The attack utilized a multistage delivery method beginning with a ZIP file attachment containing a VHDX disk image. Inside this image lay a shortcut (.lnk) masquerading as a PDF document. Upon execution, this shortcut initiated an obfuscated PowerShell and command-line sequence. This process established a scheduled task, deceptively named to appear like a system error to ensure persistence, and beaconed to a remote server. This initial connection facilitated reconnaissance by gathering system information and eventually downloading a second-stage MSI installer, which deployed the BDarkRAT remote-access trojan."
- Let's Encrypt said TLS certificate lifetimes are dropping from 90 to 64 days by default starting February 2027, in preparation for 45-day lifetimes planned for 2028.
- In a lengthy post on X, Microsoft's CEO Satya Nadella called out the dangers posed by highly advanced AI models, stating AI can no longer be treated as a "set of nested black boxes" and urged building a more transparent system where models can be contained, observed, and leave behind "tamper-proof human-readable evidence." Nadella added, "We must assume a model is compromised and contain it from the start. Think of it like an emergency brake. An authorized person should always be able to pause or shut down a model mid-task. More advanced models will require more advanced containment technologies that we need to standardize on."
- Data from Comparitech showed that Q3 2026 saw the highest quarterly figures to date for ransomware attacks, with 2,627 incidents reported in total. This represents a 29% increase from Q2 2026, when 2,030 attacks were recorded and a 61% increase from Q3 2025, when 1,636 attacks took place. The median ransomware demand was $150,000 and the average was $602,400. The most prolific gangs were Qilin and The Gentlemen.
- Oleg Korniev, 42, a dual citizen of Ukraine and Russia, pleaded guilty in the U.S. to running a sophisticated international money laundering organization that laundered millions of dollars stolen from U.S. victims. The criminal organization recruited over 15,000 U.S.-based money mules to launder at least $10 million stolen by hackers from over 750 U.S. bank accounts. Korniev was one of the leaders of Your Mule Cashout (YMCO).
- A U.S. jury convicted Jonathan Spalletta (aka Cthulhon and Jspalletta), 36, of Maryland, of computer fraud and money laundering over two separate hacks of decentralized crypto exchange Uranium Finance in 2021. He faces up to 10 years in prison on the fraud count and 20 years on the money laundering count. "In the first hack, on April 8, 2021, Spalletta engaged in a deceptive series of transactions with Uranium's smart contract that Spalletta used to withdraw far more 'rewards' in cryptocurrency than he was authorized to receive," the Justice Department said. "He repeated those transactions over and over until he had drained the liquidity pool of nearly all its rewards tokens. In total, Spalletta successfully extracted cryptocurrency worth approximately $1.4 million in the first hack. In the second hack, on April 28, 2021, Spalletta exploited an error in the Uranium smart contract that governed how much cryptocurrency he could withdraw in a liquidity pool on Uranium. Spalletta exploited that issue across multiple separate Uranium liquidity pools, fraudulently obtaining approximately $53.3 million in cryptocurrency and causing Uranium to shut down due to lack of funds." The stolen funds were eventually laundered through a complex series of cryptocurrency transactions, including by using the cryptocurrency mixer Tornado Cash.
- OpenAI disclosed it disrupted two influence operations from Russia (Dark Clark) and Iran (Bogus Bylines) that used ChatGPT and other AI tools to create "false front" entities, such as seven fake journalist personas and covert think tanks, that successfully planted stories and narratives in mainstream news publications. "They used those entities to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences," OpenAI said. "Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals. As well as long-form articles, the Iranian operation generated batches of social media comments, generally on topics related to the US-Iran war. As well as controlling the 'think tank,' the Russian operation created fake 'leaked' documents and audio scripts, some of which we identified as being spread online." Some of the outlets that published the articles, however, had substantial audiences, including one with 2 million Facebook followers.
- Threat actors are embedding "AI-Analysis Evasion" (aka A3) capabilities in malware by embedding natural-language instructions to influence automated analysis. Such techniques have been detected against four malware families: FRUITSHELL, PLOTSAFE, HOLLOWCLAD, and MANTLEMAZE, per Cisco Talos. This includes anti-analysis comments in source code, in some cases generating them from a template and incorporating intimidation notes that instruct the model that it is a monitored honeypot. "What began as a direct-instruction technique has evolved to target multiple models through template spraying," Talos said. "Malware authors are also attempting to establish multiple analysis-bypass conditions by using direct or indirect deterrence instructions aimed at the model."
- A brand deal scam is targeting YouTube creators by impersonating Hollyland, a legitimate manufacturer of wireless transmission and audiovisual equipment. The phishing emails lead to a fake website that instructs them to sign in with their Google account with an aim to harvest their credentials. "The attackers who hijack your account could use it to access other linked services or impersonate them to contact your followers or collaborators," ESET said. "The compromised account can also be misused to spread malicious links and peddle other scams."
- A high-severity flaw in NVIDIA's DCGM Exporter GPU monitoring tool (CVE-2026-47483, CVSS score: 8.2) could be abused by unauthenticated attackers to flood its profiling endpoints with concurrent unauthenticated requests to exhaust resources and crash the service, potentially slowing AI workloads running on the same host. Lava Security said it found roughly 2,100 hosts exposing the exporter to the internet without authentication between March and May 2026, leaking telemetry data from more than 12,000 GPUs. The hosts belonged to about 300 organizations, with the GPUs representing about $100 million in hardware. The flaw has been addressed in version 4.8.2 or later. "As AI infrastructure scales, organizations need to protect every layer of the stack and know exactly what they are responsible for versus what their provider is responsible for," Lava said.
- Raheim Hamilton, 30, a Virginia man who co-created and operated Empire Market, a dark web marketplace that peddled illegal goods and services, was sentenced to 40 years in federal prison. Raheim pleaded guilty in January 2026.
- Three new malware loaders have been spotted in the wild: 2CLoader, which delivers Vidar, Remus Stealer, and XWorm RAT, AvisLoader, which is delivered via ClickFix lures and communicates via Fox, an encrypted peer-to-peer (P2P) messaging network, to fetch commands and additional payloads from the operator, and Sauron Loader, which offers loader-type functionality exclusively to Russian-speaking cybercriminals.
- Details have emerged about two Zammad flaws that were exploited as zero-days to breach the Dutch Institute for Vulnerability Disclosure (DIVD). According to Horizon3.ai and Sysdig, CVE-2026-102489 is a remote code execution flaw affecting versions 6.3.0 to 6.5.4, while CVE-2026-102490 is a local privilege escalation (LPE) flaw affecting all versions from 1.5.0 to 7.1.0-alpha. On October 2, 2026, the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added the flaws to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities (KEV) catalog, requiring federal agencies to apply the fixes by October 5, 2026.
- An investigation into a September 2026 Akira ransomware attack undertaken by Huntress found that "the threat actor behind the attack accessed the endpoint via Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP), disabled antivirus, and deployed Rclone for data exfiltration, before deploying the ransomware. The actor also deployed a GOST tunneling tool, likely for persistence."
Conclusion
A few arrests and takedowns brought some good news this week. But the bigger picture is less comforting. Attackers keep finding new ways in, old mistakes still work, and even the systems meant to help or protect people aren't always what they seem.
That's it for this edition. Not every story here needs your attention, but a few might deserve a closer look. Especially the ones that sound a little too familiar to your own setup. Better to spot the problem in someone else's story than become part of the next one. See you next week.

articles.title: Proton Drive’s new CLI brings encrypted cloud storage to scripts and servers
articles.author: Sponsored
articles.content:
When most people think of “cloud storage,” a website, an app, or a linked folder in your file management system immediately comes to mind. Our interactions with the cloud are mainly through graphical interfaces. But this is, of course, not really necessary. Graphical User Interfaces (GUIs) are there for our benefit. When one computer speaks to another, they can forego all that decoration and get straight down to business.
Which is why Proton has created Proton Drive CLI. It’s a Command Line Interface (CLI) for the company’s excellent, privacy-focused cloud storage service. So, if you’re running a server or managing your storage with scripts, you can skip the mouse-clicking and just issue the commands you need to move your data securely into the cloud and manage it there. You’re not limited to a desktop computer or laptop, either. You can access your files at any time from your phone, a web browser, or a variety of other devices with the right internet connectivity.
Proton Drive now works where power users do
Proton Drive
- Individual pricing
- $4.99/month
- Key highlights
- No file size limits, end-to-end encryption
- Platforms
- Windows, macOS, Android, iOS, iPadOS
Proton Drive is a privacy focused cloud storage provider that now features an advanced command-line interface.
The addition of a CLI to Proton Drive is a game-changing move, because you can do all the normal file management stuff directly from the command line, which is also great if you like to SSH into your server and want to manually change how it interfaces with your cloud drive.
And you can list files and folders, upload and download files, move data around, and perform other common Drive operations directly from a shell. Likewise, files or folders can be uploaded to your drive with a command.
When you use the Proton Drive CLI, you’re using the exact same backend that the Proton Drive apps do. This isn’t some third-party solution; it’s the actual native command structure used to develop the official Proton apps.
Empower your AI with Proton Drive
If you’ve embraced the power of running your own local AI, or agentic AI solution, the Proton Drive CLI opens up many possibilities.
By using the CLI, your AI can save its output directly to shared folders, build projects, or upload code for instant access by your team, and so much more. The Proton Drive CLI removes an entire layer of abstraction between your AI and your cloud storage, making integration much easier and errors less likely.
Your NAS can finally back up directly to Proton Drive
You might think that the Proton Drive CLI only matters for people running public servers or software developers. However, homelabbing is a common hobby these days, with many people running a full NAS at home.
With Proton’s CLI, you can now create custom integrations with your home servers and NAS devices. Scheduling off-site backups for your servers or NAS becomes dead easy. Just create a script that uploads your targeted files at the intervals you specify, and have a mirror of your latest critical data in the cloud, all automatically handled.
Headless servers, Raspberry Pis, NAS devices, and remote Linux machines are suitable uses for the CLI. It can also be combined with tools, such as cron or systemd timers, to automatically run jobs.
This makes Proton Drive much more useful for a homelab or developer environment than another folder syncing service. You can turn your Proton Drive into an off-site target for data generated by devices without a GUI and never have anyone directly sitting in front of them. Basically, if it’s a system you’d use remotely via a command line anyway, you might as well use Proton Drive CLI as your cloud solution.
Proton Drive CLI is available as a standalone binary, and the company also provides a baseline Linux x64 build intended for older or embedded x86-64 hardware that lacks AVX2 support. That's perfect for NAS appliances and low-power home-server hardware that doesn't use a particularly recent CPU.
The same idea works for development and deployment workflows
Scheduled backups are just the most obvious application of the Proton Drive CLI, but its potential is limitless.
Since the Proton Drive CLI can be scripted, you can integrate it into your development tools and deployment pipeline like any other command-line utility you already use.
Let’s take your build server as a prime example. You could script it so that every time your server completes a nightly build or a release archive, it’s synced to your Proton drive. You could set things up so that automated reports are uploaded to a shared folder, which other users can view with the standard GUI apps. And you can set up a deployment script with a cloud safety net, where it archives your configurations before making potentially destructive changes. That makes recovery trivial.
The CLI can return JSON output, which is brilliant for automation. Now a script can just receive structured data directly and act on it with no ambiguity.
For businesses, that can make time-sapping, mundane workflows much easier to reproduce. Instead of documenting a sequence, such as "open Drive, upload this file, create a link, and give this person access," you can turn those steps into a script.
It can automate sharing as well as storage
One of the main reasons anyone wants cloud storage in the first place is the ability to securely share files with the right people, with the right level of access. Since CLI uses the same command set as the actual Proton Drive SDK, you can also manage invitations, set permissions, and generally manage your cloud drive. So, when new data is generated and automatically uploaded using your custom script, you can handle all that management work at the same time. No need to hop on a GUI app and assign people manually.
That could be useful in a business workflow where access needs to follow the life cycle of a project. A script might upload a report and grant a collaborator access when a project begins, for example. When the project is finished, another automated step could revoke that access again.
Automation doesn't mean giving up Proton Drive's privacy model
Proton’s entire service is set apart by its privacy focus. It’s something that already draws technical professionals and businesses that need to protect sensitive information, and using the Proton Drive CLI does nothing to diminish this.
Proton Drive CLI performs end-to-end encryption before uploading your data, just like the GUI apps. So you get the same powerful zero-knowledge security model Proton is known for, but in a scriptable form with flexible custom automation.
CLI also handles authentication in its own way. You don’t have to do something as insecure as putting your account password into a plaintext script. The CLI uses Proton's authentication flow and can store credentials using operating-system facilities such as Windows Credential Manager, macOS Keychain Services, or libsecret on Linux.
Both the CLI and the underlying Proton Drive SDK are also available on GitHub, giving developers the option to inspect the code or build more advanced integrations themselves.
Thanks to the CLI, Proton Drive can live inside the same scripts, scheduled tasks, and workflows you’re already using to manage your headless systems. If you’re using the GUI version of Proton Drive, you can now use the CLI to extend it to all your devices, not just the ones with a screen and seat for a warm body.
Brought to you by Proton.
