articles.title: Banks Struggle to Digest the Mounting Debt Driving the AI Boom
articles.author: Nat Wilson Turner
articles.content:
Silicon Valley is down with POTUS Trump’s rebranding of “artificial intelligence” as “super intelligence” but that hasn’t freed the “super intelligence” companies of their need for massive capital infusions.
SI, Yes AI, No
First the rebranding via The Verge:
When President Donald Trump announced his plans to rebrand artificial intelligence as “super intelligence,” you’d be forgiven for being skeptical that it would catch on. While most of the broader population is sticking with AI, some of Silicon Valley’s most powerful are falling in line and trying to give Trump the great AI rebrand he so desires.
That Elon Musk was quick to jump on board, promising to rename SpaceXAI to SpaceXSI, isn’t surprising. When, hours after Donald Trump declared that “The White House considers anyone that uses the term, ‘Artificial Intelligence,’ as opposed to the highly accepted new and more accurate term, ‘Super Intelligence,’ THE ENEMY!” Marc Benioff announced that Salesforce would rename AIForce to SIForce; it seemed like a quick capitulation, but not entirely out of character.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang attended the summit where the executive order requiring government agencies to use the term “super intelligence” was announced. He’s also aligned himself with Trump, saying he believes the danger posed by AI is overblown. So it was somewhat predictable that when Nvidia declared that it would “commit” $1 billion to scientific advancement, that included “super intelligence research.” Of course, Huang has a lot to lose if he gets on Trump’s bad side.
The latest to cave is Microsoft’s Satya Nadella, who attended the same AI summit as Huang along with Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jeff Bezos, Dario Amodei, and Musk. In a post calling for building an “emergency brake” for AI yesterday, Nadella repeatedly referred to the technology as “super intelligence.”
As much as you’d think this name change would be revolutionary, it doesn’t appear to have impacted balance sheets.
Capital Is the Tech Bottleneck
Tech titans gathered at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday and the consensus was clear: capital not hardware is the biggest bottleneck facing the industry.
Broadcom CEO Hock Tan said financing could become a bigger obstacle to AI expansion than shortages of semiconductors, memory chips or electricity, as the industry races to build the infrastructure needed to power increasingly sophisticated models.
″[What] I think might be the biggest constraint is capital,” Hock Tan said at the DBS Asia Future Forward Conference in Singapore on Monday.
Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan echoed concerns about financing, pointing to the rising cost of capital and questions over whether companies investing heavily in AI will eventually generate sufficient returns.
“If there’s any challenge in the front, it’s capital and the cost of capital, and then the other part is in the longer run, people want to see the ROI,” he said.
Their remarks highlight an emerging challenge for the AI industry, which has poured enormous sums into data centers, advanced chips and power infrastructure in anticipation of surging demand for computing capacity.
The warnings come as rising borrowing costs threaten to complicate financing for technology companies investing heavily in AI infrastructure. Higher bond yields could make it more expensive to fund data center construction and chip purchases, potentially putting pressure on the economics of projects that may take years to generate returns.
How much debt are we talking about? This much debt:
|  | Debt ($bn) | Leases not started ($bn) | Guarantees ($bn) | 2026 bonds ($bn) | 
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Oracle | 125.3 | 288 | 3.3 | 25 | 
| Meta | 84.0 | 279+68 | 28+13 | 25 | 
| Alphabet | 101.1 | 85.2 | 43.8 | 51.8+25 | 
| Microsoft | 46.1 | 329.1 | 0 | 0 | 
| Amazon | 133.0 | 137.2 | 0 | 82.4+5.8 | 
| Nvidia | 33.4 | 25+20 | 108.5 | 25 | 
| CoreWeave | 35.6 | 35.5 | — | — | 
AI debt has gotten so massive that the Financial Times asked “Are Big Tech bonds crowding out the US Treasury?”
And while the answer is likely, “no”, this chart from the article shows that AI-related debt is going up dramatically and quickly:
https://t.co/eFT7jEnnlg
— Nat Wilson Turner (@natwilsonturner) October 12, 2026
JPMorgan Asset Management’s Michael Cembalest has also created an alarming arrow go up and to the right graph:
https://t.co/BpkiPipJU3
— Nat Wilson Turner (@natwilsonturner) October 12, 2026
The total capital raised by hyperscalers, data center special-purpose vehicles, and neo-clouds in the form of investment-grade debt, high-yield debt, and equity capital rose from $172 billion in 2025 to $346 billion thus far in 2026, an increase of more than 100%, per new research from Barclays strategist Venu Krishna on Wednesday.
…
On the debt front, Alphabet (GOOG, GOOGL), Amazon (AMZN), Meta (META), Microsoft (MSFT), and Oracle (ORCL) collectively raised about $159 billion in bonds through early June 2026 — a 47% increase from what these companies issued all of last year.
Alphabet, for instance, became the first tech company in decades to issue a 100-year bond, raising $31.51 billion in February across its global bond offering.
https://t.co/rWAKMgjE3l
— Nat Wilson Turner (@natwilsonturner) October 12, 2026
Michael Burry and others have also been alarmed by the amount of off-balance-sheet liability the hyperscalers have accrued. As Axios reported in August, citing Morgan Stanley:
Morgan Stanley looked at filings from the hyperscalers Google, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle and Amazon, as well as the chipmakers Nvidia and Broadcom and broke down their off-balance-sheet commitments.
The hyperscalers have committed to $1.1 trillion in payments for data center leases that haven’t yet begun.
All seven companies have also agreed to buy $1.7 trillion of other stuff — purchase commitments for chips, memory and networking gear.
These purchase agreements have ramped up this year — Google’s commitments totaled $707 billion in the most recent quarter — from $72.5 billion in all of 2025, per the research.
https://t.co/u3hW8iaJPd
— Nat Wilson Turner (@natwilsonturner) October 12, 2026
Those off-balance-sheet obligations are real debt, and it trades. The structure works like this: a special purpose vehicle (SPV), mostly owned by an asset manager, borrows the money, builds the data center and leases it to the tech company. The tech company books the rent as a lease. The bonds sit with the SPV. Prices on those bonds have been sliding.
- Meta, Hyperion (Louisiana): Beignet Investor LLC, 80% owned by Blue Owl funds and 20% by Meta, sold $27bn of 6.581% bonds due 2049 in October 2025. Pimco bought about $18bn of them and BlackRock ETFs more than $3bn. On 28 September the bonds traded at 91 cents on the dollar, a 7.55% yield, about 230 basis points over Treasuries versus 185 at launch, and they hit a record low on 7 October. Meta signed four-year initial leases with options to renew for up to 20 years. It also gave a residual value guarantee of about $28bn: if Meta leaves and the campus is worth less than an agreed amount, Meta covers the shortfall up to that figure. Meta calls a payout “not probable” and records no liability. S&P rated the bonds A+ but warned that substantial credit risk passes back to Meta.
- Meta, El Paso (Texas): Sopaipilla Investor LLC, 80% owned by BlackRock funds and 20% by Meta, sold $12.5bn of 7.534% bonds due 2048 in July, priced 287.5 basis points over Treasuries. Bloomberg called that yield “a level more common in junk bonds” and said demand was “tepid by one standard measure.” Meta’s residual value guarantee on El Paso is about $13bn.
- Microsoft, QTS (Georgia): Microsoft has sold no bonds of its own in two fiscal years but has $329.1bn of data-center leases signed and not yet started. Its landlords do the borrowing. Blackstone’s QTS sold about $3.9bn of five-year bonds in August for a Microsoft-leased Georgia project, at a yield in the low-to-mid 7% range, comparable to single-B junk. Bloomberg’s headline: “Bond Traders Bite at Microsoft-Tied Data Center Junk-Like Yields.” In April a QTS bond refinancing its Fayetteville, Georgia campus, where Microsoft is the tenant, raised $4.6bn.
Not Just the HyperScalers, the Banks Too
Barclays pointed out this week that the banks are following big tech into debt. Per Bloomberg:
Analysts from Barclays Plc estimate the six largest US banks will tap the debt market for about $41 billion in the current quarter, an amount that would be 30% above the fourth-quarter average going back to 2015. In the third quarter, senior debt issuance reached $50 billion, more than double prior-year levels, according to Barclays.
Banks have ramped up borrowing to finance not only the AI buildout, and the hundreds of billions being spent by hyperscalers and tech giants from SpaceX to Oracle Corp., but also to facilitate the increased trading and market activity that has cropped up in tandem with the growing industry…
Year to date, these banks have borrowed $192 billion globally, up some 40% from the same time last year, with the full-year tally estimated at $233 billion, according to the Barclays strategists. For US banks as a whole, they now forecast full-year senior debt issuance of $294 billion, some 25% higher than their initial estimate and up from $240 billion in 2025.
Among the six banks, Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, which have led 2026 issuance, may be the most active borrowers post earnings next week, said Bloomberg Intelligence analyst Arnold Kakuda.
While banks are particularly savvy when it comes to timing borrowing, a recent surge in benchmark borrowing costs may be a deterrent to adding on too much debt. Meanwhile, indications of growing credit concerns around the hyperscalers and other tech borrowers point to increasing unease over the piles of debt feeding the heavy spending on AI.
There’s another set of players in addition to the banks: private credit.
Private Credit Has Piled In
Behind the banks sits private credit: loans made directly by asset managers like Blue Owl, Apollo, Blackstone, Pimco and Brookfield, using money from pension funds, insurers and, increasingly, individual investors in non-traded funds. The loans mostly don’t trade, so their value is whatever the lender says it is. Morgan Stanley estimated in 2025 that data centers would need about $1.5tn of outside financing through 2028, with about $800bn coming from private credit. The Bank of England’s Financial Policy Committee now cites Morgan Stanley’s estimate of about $700bn of data-center spending over 2026-2028 financed by private credit.
Who’s in:
- Blue Owl owns 80% of Meta’s Hyperion campus, put about $3bn of equity into Oracle’s Project Jupiter, and is a partner in the Abilene Stargate site. Reuters reported it struggled to syndicate a $4bn CoreWeave-anchored deal in Lancaster, Pennsylvania.
- Apollo and Blackstone put up $35bn to buy chips for Anthropic, which UBS Asset Management calls the largest private credit deal on record. Blackstone is leading the $18bn junior piece of Broadcom’s new $60bn Anthropic chip package and plans to keep $9bn of it. Apollo is weighing raising its loan to SoftBank’s Vision Fund 2 from $5.4bn to $9bn to help fund SoftBank’s OpenAI commitments.
- Pimco bought about $18bn of the Hyperion bonds and about $10bn of the $14bn of bonds for Oracle’s Michigan site, then sought to sell parts of the Michigan debt.
- Nvidia signed agreements in August with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs and KKR to set up financing platforms meant to raise more than $500bn from outside investors for Nvidia’s customers.
Signs of strain:
- Blue Owl again capped withdrawals from two of its private credit funds after investors asked to pull 39% and 17% of their shares, about $4.2bn in all (2 October). Apollo capped a fund after 14.7% of investors asked to exit (22 September). Blackstone’s flagship private credit fund capped redemptions at 5% again (3 September).
- Fitch put the US private credit default rate at a record 6.3% for the year to August.
- SEC staff issued a statement on how funds value private assets on 28 September. Three days later Apollo said it would start pricing its roughly $850bn of credit assets daily.
Perhaps this is why investor demand for tech debt is rapidly declining.
Investor Demand for Tech Debt Takes a Dive
Another Bloomberg piece, titled “AI Debt Spree Hammers Tech Debt as Traders Rush to Reprice Risk.
Highlights:
The pace and sheer scale of the borrowings, combined with unknowns around the technology and rising interest rates, is put growing pressure on the sector. Tech has been among the worst-performing sectors across credit in recent months, leaving investors nursing losses, while average daily trading volumes for tech names in the bond and credit derivatives markets have soared.
In recent days, news of a wave of potential fresh financings from SpaceX and Broadcom, possibly topping $100 billion, sent credit derivatives linked to hyperscalers and chipmakers climbing to prices that suggest traders see a growing risk of a default over the next five years. For Oracle, it’s now above 20%, for SpaceX it’s about 16% — and even Nvidia Corp., the world’s most valuable company, is given a more than 7% risk of default in that time.
…
So-called mega transactions in the tens of billions of dollars used to be few and far between and syndicate banks would spend months telegraphing the deals ahead of launch, plus most of the huge deals were earmarked for mergers and acquisitions. This year, there have been nine US high-grade deals that are $25 billion or above in size, the most ever, most of them in tech.
The US high-yield market, meanwhile, is poised for one of its busiest year on record. And while debt markets have absorbed the record supply relatively well, investors are starting to demand higher compensation to lend to the sector, particularly as financing needs expand beyond the so-called hyperscalers into chip financing, data centers, and other structures, according to Steven Kohlenstein, fixed-income portfolio manager at T. Rowe Price.
https://t.co/owUnJVcm2G
— Nat Wilson Turner (@natwilsonturner) October 12, 2026
For now the issue is less about actual deterioration in credit quality than about market saturation. Most of these big borrowers are profitable, with steady cash flow and earnings momentum. And their weaker performance hasn’t spilled over into the broader market, which has held up relatively well.
These borrowers are also tapping as many corners of demand as they can, borrowing in global markets and exploring various debt structures to help mitigate risks. But even so, the crush of debt in such a relatively short span of time gives investors at least some bargaining power to demand more compensation for taking on the debt. And there are unknowns about the AI rollout, the potential payoff and the risks around the technology, all of which could upend valuations.
Among expected borrowings that have recently come to light, Broadcom is sketching out plans for its next blockbuster deal just days after it launched a $60 billion debt financing to help fund Anthropic PBC’s artificial intelligence buildout, Bloomberg reported Wednesday.
Broadcom’s five-year CDS widened by 3 basis points to a record 136 basis points on Thursday, according to ICE Data Services.
It’s quite a party, although there may be the proverbial poop in the punchbowl, in the form of delayed data centers.
Who’s Holding the Bag for Those Data Centers?
For every data center delayed by “force majeure” and otherwise, there is a counterparty holding the bag. Here’s what I can put together about who owes what for some of the bigger projects:
| Project | Debt | Banks | Status | 
|---|---|---|---|
| Project Jupiter, N.M. Oracle tenant; Blue Owl/Stack | $18bn | About 20 banks; SMBC, BNP Paribas, Goldman, MUFG agents | Quoted at 89-91 cents; Santander, Jefferies holding more than planned (18 Sep). Oracle force majeure notice 24 Sep; Morgan Stanley: weighs on data-center debt | 
| Vantage, Texas + Wisconsin Oracle tenant | $38bn | JPMorgan, MUFG lead; Wells Fargo, BNP, Goldman, SMBC, SocGen | Months to sell down; some lenders still offloading (Apr) | 
| Hubbard, Texas Anthropic tenant; Google backstop | $15bn | Morgan Stanley lead | Banks seeking to offload (FT, Aug) | 
| AI data-center loans, various | — | JPMorgan, Morgan Stanley, SMBC, MUFG | Explored loan sales and significant risk transfers (FT, May) | 
The scary part is who is ultimately on the hook to pay for these data centers. Sometimes that’s the weakest links in the chain.
Who’s On the Hook and For What?
The chipmakers and cloud giants are also guaranteeing their customers’ debt. When a lab like OpenAI or Anthropic, or a small cloud company like Fluidstack, can’t borrow on its own credit, a bigger company promises to cover the rent if the customer stops paying. The lenders are really lending against that promise. None of it shows up as debt on the guarantor’s balance sheet.
- Nvidia and OpenAI: In an 8-K filed 17 August, Nvidia agreed to guarantee up to $105bn of the value of leases OpenAI is signing for about 4.25 gigawatts at SB Energy’s campus in Pike County, Ohio. If OpenAI goes insolvent or stops paying, Nvidia pays the gap between the guaranteed lease value and whatever the landlord recovers by re-leasing or selling the site. The guarantee runs up to 20 years, and Nvidia has an option to back about 3.8 more gigawatts. The Wall Street Journal reported the talks at $250bn in July. Nvidia’s latest 10-Q puts its total maximum guarantee exposure at $108.5bn, including $3.5bn on data-center leases for smaller AI cloud companies, which it took on in exchange for warrants in those companies.
- Google: Alphabet’s 10-Q shows backstops of other companies’ data-center leases rose to $43.8bn at the end of June, from $16.9bn six months earlier, with terms of up to 15 years. It has agreed to about $24.1bn more. Google accounts for them as credit derivatives. Several of the disclosed deals back Fluidstack, a small AI cloud company, at sites owned by former bitcoin miners. Google backstopped $1.8bn of Fluidstack’s leases at TeraWulf’s Lake Mariner site, $1.3bn at TeraWulf’s Abernathy, Texas, site and $1.73bn at Cipher Mining’s Barber Lake, Texas, site, taking warrants in the miners in some of the deals. Google also backstops rent and power at Anthropic’s Hubbard, Texas, campus, where banks are lining up $15bn of debt. Bloomberg reported the backstop was needed because Anthropic has no credit rating.
- Amazon: The Financial Times reported on 2 October that Amazon is in talks to move about $8bn of Nvidia Grace Blackwell chips into an SPV that would raise debt and equity from outside investors, then lease the chips back. The chips would stay in AWS data centers. Investors expect the debt to get an investment-grade rating tied to Amazon’s own AA rating. Amazon declined to comment.
Unfortunately, there’s one other problem: free cash flow, or the lack thereof.
Free Cash Flow, My Kingdom for Free Cash Flow
Why borrow at all? These are some of the most profitable companies in the world. But the data-center bill now eats up nearly all the cash the businesses throw off. Goldman Sachs estimates the big hyperscalers will spend about $750bn on capex in 2026, against about $778bn of operating cash flow. That leaves about $28bn to spare, and Goldman expects debt to pay for about a third of capex this year.
- Amazon: Free cash flow over the trailing twelve months went negative, to -$7.6bn at the end of June, from +$18.2bn a year earlier and $25.9bn in early 2025. Capex over the same period hit $169bn, up $66bn. So Amazon borrowed: $82.4bn of new debt in the first half alone, nearly doubling its long-term debt to $133bn from $68.8bn at the end of 2025. Its 10-Q says it expects “additional financing activities in 2026,” and it sold £4.25bn of bonds in September.
- Oracle: Free cash flow was -$5.4bn in the quarter to August, after -$23.7bn for the fiscal year that ended in May. Capex was $28.5bn in the quarter, up from $8.5bn a year earlier. Interest expense rose to $1.43bn from $923m. To cover the gap Oracle sold $19.9bn of stock through an at-the-market program and took $11.4bn of prepayments from customers. S&P cut Oracle to BBB- in July, one notch above junk, and forecasts a free cash flow deficit of nearly $42bn for this fiscal year.
- Microsoft is the exception on paper. It brought in $182.9bn of operating cash in its fiscal year to June and spent $115.9bn on property and equipment, and it hasn’t sold a bond in two years. But those capex figures leave out its finance leases, which rose to $66.6bn from $46.2bn, and the $329.1bn of data-center leases it has signed that haven’t started yet.
Fun party, it would be a shame if someone took away the punchbowl.
articles.summary:
Despite a high-profile rebranding of artificial intelligence to "super intelligence" by the White House, major tech companies face mounting financial pressure due to massive capital requirements for infrastructure.

### Key Points
- Tech giants including Microsoft, Alphabet, and Meta have collectively raised over $159 billion in bonds through mid-2026, a 47% increase over the previous year.
- Hyperscalers have accrued over $1.1 trillion in off-balance-sheet commitments for future data center leases and $1.7 trillion in purchase obligations for hardware.
- Industry leaders like Broadcom CEO Hock Tan and Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan identified capital availability and rising borrowing costs as the primary bottlenecks for AI expansion.
- Private credit firms, including Blackstone and Apollo, are increasingly financing AI infrastructure, though rising default rates and withdrawal caps signal growing market strain.
- Goldman Sachs estimates that 2026 capital expenditures for major hyperscalers will reach $750 billion, nearly exhausting their combined operating cash flow.

### Why it Matters
The reliance on massive debt and off-balance-sheet financing to fund AI infrastructure creates significant systemic risk if the expected returns on these investments fail to materialize. As borrowing costs rise and investor demand for tech debt cools, the industry's aggressive expansion strategy faces a potential liquidity crunch that could impact both tech balance sheets and the broader financial markets.

articles.title: The New Non-Negotiable for Small Businesses? Knowing Your Cyber Risk. Here’s Where to Begin.
articles.author: Mark Barnett
articles.content:
Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.
Key Takeaways
- For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), a cyberattack can disrupt operations, damage customer trust and even threaten the company’s survival.
- The most successful businesses won’t just be the ones that respond effectively when an attack occurs. They’ll be the ones that build resilience into the way they operate from the beginning.
- Many SMEs don’t have the resources to employ dedicated cybersecurity teams. They need guidance that is practical, actionable and integrated into tools they already use every day.
- When security is accessible and integrated into the tools they already use, entrepreneurs can address risks earlier and move forward with greater confidence.
Every small business starts with a dream.
Whether it’s expanding into a new market, hiring a first employee or turning a side hustle into a lasting business, growth is what motivates entrepreneurs to take risks and build something of their own. But dreams only grow when the day-to-day works, when customers trust the business, operations run smoothly and unexpected setbacks don’t derail progress.
That’s why cybersecurity is no longer just an IT issue. For small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), cybersecurity is now fundamental to building trust, serving customers and growing with confidence.
As SMEs become more digital, they gain new opportunities to scale, streamline operations and serve customers more effectively. But digital transformation can be a double-edged sword: As impactful as it is, it also invites new forms of risk. Increasingly, understanding cyber risk is becoming just as important as understanding cash flow, customer acquisition or inventory management.
The most successful businesses won’t simply be the ones that respond effectively when an attack occurs. They’ll be the ones that build resilience into the way they operate from the beginning.
Cyber risk is becoming part of the growth journey
Small businesses today rely on digital tools at nearly every stage of their operations. They use cloud-based software to manage workflows, digital channels to acquire customers, online payment systems to facilitate transactions and connected platforms to collaborate with suppliers and partners.
This shift has created tremendous opportunities. Business owners can reach new customers, automate routine tasks and make more informed decisions than ever before.
But increased connectivity also means increased exposure.
For many entrepreneurs, a cyber incident can have consequences that extend far beyond the initial attack. A breach can disrupt operations, prevent a business from accepting payments, compromise customer information, delay order fulfillment or interrupt payroll. Trust that may have taken years to build can be damaged in a matter of hours.
The impact can be especially severe for smaller organizations that often lack dedicated security teams or specialized expertise.
Mastercard’s Global SME Cybersecurity Landscape research found that 46% of SMEs say their current business has experienced a cyberattack. Even more concerning, nearly one in five business owners whose companies experienced an attack reported subsequently filing for bankruptcy (18%) or closing their business (17%).
These statistics underscore an important reality: Cybersecurity is no longer solely about protecting systems. It is about protecting a business’s ability to operate, grow and earn customer trust.
Cybersecurity as a growth enabler
One of the clearest findings from Mastercard’s Dreamonomics research, based on a survey of more than 6,600 SMEs across 18 markets, is that entrepreneurs are redefining what growth means. Increasingly, business owners are prioritizing stability, predictability and long-term sustainability alongside expansion. The most successful businesses are pursuing what could be described as controlled momentum: growth that is resilient and built to last.
In that environment, cybersecurity is becoming less about defense alone and more about enabling confidence.
That same research found that 71% of small businesses prioritize protection from cyber threats, yet only 37% currently use cybersecurity tools.
That gap is revealing.
Business owners recognize cybersecurity as important, but many still struggle to find solutions that are accessible, practical and relevant to the realities of running a small business.
The signal is clear: Entrepreneurs increasingly want smarter, simpler ways to understand and manage cyber risk without becoming cybersecurity experts themselves.
In many ways, cybersecurity is following the same trajectory as other business functions. Owners don’t necessarily want more technology to manage. They want solutions that reduce complexity and help them make better decisions with confidence.
Why reactive cybersecurity falls short
Historically, many businesses have approached cybersecurity only after something goes wrong.
An attack occurs. A breach is discovered. Systems go down. Then the work of recovery begins. But recovery is often more expensive, disruptive and time-consuming than prevention.
As cyber threats become more sophisticated, the conversation is increasingly shifting from “How do we recover?” to “How do we identify risks before they become problems?”
This is a fundamentally different mindset.
Instead of treating cybersecurity as a response plan, businesses are beginning to view it as an ongoing capability that supports operational resilience and long-term growth.
The goal is not to eliminate every risk. No business can do that. The goal is to understand where vulnerabilities exist, prioritize the issues that matter most and take practical steps to address them before they become costly disruptions.
How SMEs can embed security into everyday business
One of the biggest opportunities facing the industry today is making cybersecurity easier for small businesses to understand and act upon.
Many entrepreneurs don’t have the resources to employ dedicated cybersecurity teams. They need guidance that is practical, actionable and integrated into tools they already use every day.
This is where a growing number of financial institutions and technology providers are beginning to play a larger role. Rather than treating cybersecurity as a standalone service, providers are increasingly embedding protection directly into the products and experiences business owners already rely on.
That’s exactly why Mastercard integrated MyCyberRisk — a proactive risk assessment tool that enables businesses to pinpoint, prioritize and act on cybersecurity threats — into The Mastercard Collection for Business. Designed around the evolving needs of modern entrepreneurs, The Mastercard Collection for Business brings together growth resources, premium experiences and cybersecurity support in a single, connected offering.
It was designed to reflect a simple reality: Business owners shouldn’t have to choose between pursuing growth and protecting what they’ve built. When security is accessible and integrated into the tools they already use, entrepreneurs can address risks earlier and move forward with greater confidence.
Smarter security, stronger businesses
Every small business starts with a dream. But dreams need more than ambition to succeed.
They need resilience. They need trust. They need the confidence that comes from knowing the business can withstand unexpected challenges and continue moving forward.
Cybersecurity has become an essential part of that foundation.
For SMEs, the most important first steps often include understanding where the business is exposed, prioritizing vulnerabilities that could create the greatest operational impact and building protection into existing workflows wherever possible.
When business owners understand where they are vulnerable and have access to tools that help them proactively address risk, security becomes more than protection. It becomes an enabler of innovation. It helps organizations adopt new technologies with greater confidence, serve customers more effectively and scale without introducing unnecessary risk.
Small businesses shouldn’t need cybersecurity teams to understand where they are vulnerable. The next step for the industry is to make cyber protection simpler, more accessible and more deeply integrated into the services entrepreneurs already use to run their businesses.
Because ultimately, the businesses best positioned for what’s next won’t simply be the ones that respond to cyber threats. They’ll be the ones that build trust, resilience and security into the way they grow, protecting what they’ve built while creating the confidence to pursue what comes next.
Key Takeaways

articles.title: I tested ASUS' Googlebook 14: So, how does it feel to a lifelong Windows user?
articles.author: ben.wilson@windowscentral.com (Ben Wilson) , Ben Wilson
articles.content:
In September this year, Google announced its 'Googlebooks' as a premium laptop counterpart to its budget-conscious Chromebooks, rather than a replacement. It wouldn't have made much of a blip on my radar if the company hadn't paired with some of my favorite OEMs to build them.
Indeed, Google isn't building any first-party devices. Unlike Chromebook, these new Android-based offerings come only from OEMs like Acer, ASUS, Dell, HP, and Lenovo. 14-inch Windows laptops have quickly become my favorite, with ASUS' Zenbook in the lead, so the $1,299 ASUS Googlebook 14 is intriguing.
Admittedly, that mild intrigue is tempered by skepticism, given the ongoing controversy over app compatibility for the average consumer. I still see people blasting Windows on ARM devices as an inferior experience, despite Qualcomm's efforts with Snapdragon X2 chips proving that to be largely false.
With that in mind, could I ever seriously expect the general public to adopt another operating system with fewer features than Windows, less customization than Linux, and some pricing sensibilities of Mac? Offered a chance to test-drive a sample from ASUS, I couldn't resist. Here's how it went.
ASUS Googlebook 14: What I like
The ASUS Googlebook 14 looks (and feels) great, which didn't surprise me, given how much I've enjoyed the company's recent design evolutions. Its chassis is coated in a magnesium-aluminum alloy, which explicitly avoids being labeled as the same Ceraluminum as its Zenbooks, but it's extremely similar.
Perhaps most impressive is its weight; ASUS claims the Googlebook 14 starts at 0.99 kg (2.18 lbs), but my scales place it closer to 0.97 kg (2.13 lbs). I'm a big fan of this emerging trend, having adored the Zenbook A14 at 2.18 lbs. Yes, it comes with extra screen flex, but I don't make a habit of bending my laptops.
OLED displays rarely disappoint either, and sure enough, this 16:10 panel also looks great. I'm still getting used to matte screens, and frankly, I almost want to avoid touching it to prevent fingerprints. Nevertheless, it's rated for up to 450 nits of brightness and 100% DCI-P3 color gamut coverage. Good for creators.
Finally, the chiclet keyboard has a 1.5mm key travel, which is relatively deep and feels good enough. The 6-inch haptic touchpad, however, is immediately fantastic. Left-clicking works anywhere, and it responds convincingly when pressed. I'll even commend the I/O for keeping USB-A ports around.
ASUS Googlebook 14: What I don't like
Before I had a chance to experience much of Googlebook OS (which can refer to itself as ChromeOS during setup), I was irked by a few user experience oddities. Granted, these are primarily related to my expectations as a Windows user, but when I pressed the Caps Lock button, I expected capital letters.
Instead, Caps Lock defaults to activating a context menu indicated by a plus (+) icon, a sort of one-size-fits-all window that resembles Microsoft's 'Emoji and more' picker. Pressing Fn + Caps Lock delivers what I really wanted, which should be no big deal, just a learning curve. But it keeps going.
There's no delete key, so I need Fn + Backspace for that, which I wouldn't mind if double-tapping the touchpad would drag to select multiple words, but it doesn't work that way; I can only double-tap one word at a time. I suppose I might get used to that, too. Shift + arrow keys still select full lines, after all.
Some aren't as drastic; a single haptic click at the top of an app with maintained contact allows me to drag it around, while double-tapping restores or maximizes as I'd expect. On the other hand, there's no right-click area by default, instead requiring a two-finger tap unless I toggle that touchpad tweak in Settings.
Again, most of these gripes can be so easily dismissed as nothingburger preferences carried over from decades of habits formed on Windows, which is fair, but trying to carry out my daily workflow on the ASUS Googlebook 14 soon had me wondering how much broad appeal this platform will have.
Like an Android smartphone, Google supplies your apps from the Play Store. Starting with Slack shows how a Googlebook handles compatibility by dividing apps into categories ranked from best to worst: Made for desktop, Optimized for desktop, Compatible with desktop, Better on the website, and Built for mobile.
Slack feels like an unlucky starting place for my Googlebook adventure since it lands in the 'Better on the website' category, made worse by a message that says, "This app cannot be installed" as a PWA (Progressive Web App). Installing it anyway is, indeed, a lesser experience than using it in Chrome.
Opening the 'Compatible with desktop' Microsoft Edge brings the entire Googlebook to a strange halt, preventing even Task Manager from opening until I restart, and my chosen video editing suite, DaVinci Resolve, isn't available at all. I know it's in its infancy, but Google's OS isn't thrilling me so far.
ASUS Googlebook 14: What happens next?
All of these impressions came in the first 24 hours of having my hands on this interesting, AI-centric laptop, and there's more to see. Gemini begs me to use it at every turn, but my next step is syncing my Pixel 7 Pro or Galaxy Z Flip 7 to see how features like 'Cast my apps' actually perform.
I'm not writing it off yet, but my first impressions aren't exactly stellar. Even the RGB Glowbar gimmick offers little more than battery-life visibility; almost as frivolous as the illuminated "look what I have" logos on gaming laptop lids. On the software side, OS updates will likely fix many of my complaints.
Still, I won't ignore the outspoken Windows users who have pushed back on Copilot AI integrations in Microsoft's leading OS for the past few years, and I can only wonder who would adopt something fundamentally the same, except built by Google. Are Googlebooks perhaps only appealing to developers?
Either way, I'm impressed with ASUS but unconvinced by Googlebook. The hardware is fantastic, but it comes from the same people who built the Zenbook, so that's hardly a revelation. I'll keep using Googlebook OS for a few more days and see how it feels once the launch hype dies down.
Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more.
Ben is a Senior Editor of Windows Central, covering PC gaming hardware, software, and everything connected to it. He's built more custom desktops than he can count, and has hands-on experience with some of the most exciting components and accessories for Windows PC and Xbox. A lifelong obsession with Microsoft's technology has led to broad expertise in laptops and in the cutting-edge processors that are pushing the industry forward.

articles.title: Sportsbooks Face New York Scrutiny Over AI and At-Risk Bettors
articles.author: ReadWrite
articles.content:
New York’s Gaming Commission unanimously advanced proposals to restrict how licensed mobile sportsbooks use AI to personalize promotions and wagering advice, alongside new requirements to identify and contact patrons who may be at risk of problem gambling.
The revised measures remain proposals, not rules in effect. The commission’s action puts both marketing systems and operator responses to risky betting behavior into the next stage of state review.
Proposals target personalization and at-risk bettors
The AI measure would restrict sportsbooks, their affiliates and vendors from using artificial intelligence, algorithmic profiling, machine learning, generative systems or other automated decision tools to analyze customer data and tailor promotions, bonuses, odds, betting limits, messages or product recommendations. It would also bar operators from suggesting particular wagers, types of bets or betting amounts.
The proposal would prohibit promotions intended to increase customers’ spending, revenue or engagement. It would not apply to parimutuel horse racing; the commission’s account also describes a customer-consent exception, but does not specify its scope.
A separate proposal would require licensees to identify customers who may be at risk of problem-gambling behavior and assign a person to engage them about those behaviors and related issues. New York has nine licensed mobile operators: Bally Bet, BetMGM, Caesars Sportsbook, DraftKings, Fanatics, FanDuel, Resorts World Bet, Rush Street Interactive and theScore Bet. The state taxes mobile sports-betting gross gaming revenue at 51%.
Commission flags gaps between operators
Commission Chairman Brian O’Dwyer raised the risk that a customer restricted by one sportsbook could simply move to another licensed operator. He urged companies to work together and share data so that customers could not avoid intervention by switching platforms.
“The industry is on notice by me and this Commission that they need to solve this problem,” O’Dwyer said. “It’s a problem that this Commission will require to be addressed and if the industry does not address it, then we will address it, and they may not like it or the solution we come up with.”
The measures were included in Gov. Kathy Hochul’s 2026 State of the State program, announced in March, which addressed underage gambling, marketing to at-risk customers and gambling addiction. New York’s AI proposal draws on a similar New Jersey regulation, according to CDC Gaming, but does not amount to an outright ban on the technology.
The New York action is part of a wider debate over how sportsbooks use customer data in marketing and how regulators should respond to gambling-related risks. ProPublica reported that the commission’s proposed rules would adopt specific thresholds for identifying at-risk bettors, followed by a required check-in; the details could change as the proposals proceed.
Industry says regulated market remains central
Sports Betting Alliance President Joe Maloney said the group would continue working with regulators to ensure the proposals strengthen New York’s regulated market. He also described licensed operators as accountable to state regulators for consumer protection, responsibility and integrity.
“Since 2022, New Yorkers aged 21 plus have been able to place legal wagers in a trusted, regulated market with licensed operators held to account by regulators that ensure commitments to consumer protection, responsibility, and integrity,” Maloney said in a statement.
Maloney also said the legal framework had ended the illegal market’s monopoly and that regulated operators now generate more than $1 billion annually in tax revenue. Those figures are the alliance president’s characterization of the market, not a commission finding cited in the reporting.
The revised AI rules will receive additional public comment before returning to the commission for discussion and a possible vote. Regulators have not set a date for a final vote, leaving room for further changes before any requirements take effect.

The New York State Gaming Commission has advanced new proposals to restrict how mobile sportsbooks use artificial intelligence for personalized marketing and to mandate interventions for at-risk bettors.

### Key Points
- The proposed rules would prohibit sportsbooks from using AI to tailor promotions, odds, or betting suggestions to individual customers.
- Operators would be required to identify customers exhibiting signs of problem gambling and assign personnel to engage them directly.
- Nine licensed mobile operators, including FanDuel, DraftKings, and BetMGM, would be subject to these new regulatory standards.
- Commission Chairman Brian O’Dwyer urged operators to share data to prevent at-risk gamblers from simply switching to different betting platforms.
- The measures align with Governor Kathy Hochul’s 2026 State of the State program, which prioritizes addressing gambling addiction and marketing practices.

### Why it Matters
These proposals represent a significant shift in how regulators oversee the intersection of data-driven marketing and consumer protection in the sports betting industry. By limiting algorithmic personalization, New York aims to curb aggressive engagement tactics that may exacerbate gambling addiction among vulnerable users.

articles.title: 10 Times Software Got Users In Trouble With The US Government
articles.author: staff@bgr.com (Joel Loynds)
articles.content:
10 Times Software Got Users In Trouble With The US Government
Every once in a while, software manages to land users in hot water. Recently, and most unprecedented, was the case of Sam Tunick, an activist connected to the resistance against "Cop City," a training facility in Atlanta. While being held by American law enforcement, he wiped his phone with Android alternative GrapheneOS' duress security feature, which wipes the phone completely and prevents recovery. It is legally unprecedented, and the U.S. government is now using a federal statute that prohibits the destruction of property to prevent its seizure in an investigation against the operating system's core functionality. The case is ongoing, but it's not the first time the government has had a problem with how people use software.
Parallels can be drawn between the government's stance on GrapheneOS and the massive amount of hacking and cybersecurity attacks targeting businesses and their general user bases, which have risen considerably in the last few years. Cody Kretsinger was sent to prison for a year for hacking Sony Pictures in 2011. On his eponymous website, Kretsinger described it as a "period of arrogance, recklessness, and consequence," which unveiled swaths of passwords and confidential information using a SQL injection.
SQL injections are among the more common cyberattacks. It's a method of manipulating input to a database and forcing it to execute malicious commands. Hackers can use SQL Injection to dump the database or tamper with information. In 2007 and 2009, the Turkish hacker collective "m0sted" breached the U.S. Army's servers and got away with it.
The U.S. government has been looking to backdoor encryption
U.S. government bodies have bungled operations in the cybersecurity world in weird ways. In 2019, two pentesters, I.T. professionals who test for vulnerabilities in various situations, were arrested for performing a "red-team" exercise on the Iowa Judicial Branch. What the branch didn't know was that they'd been given permission to breach the system and were awarded $600,000 in January 2026 for defamation and wrongful arrest.
Security on user devices has been under attack by the U.S. government in general, especially in 2025. As the Electronic Freedom Foundation reported, the STOP CSAM Act threatens to introduce a backdoor into encrypted messaging services, like WhatsApp and Signal, so that information being sent is certified not to contain sexually exploitative content involving children. It is currently pending legislation. The U.S. government has butted heads with Apple in the past over encryption.
In 2016, the FBI wanted Apple to provide software to crack open phones and break through encryption provided by apps and software. It also requested the capability to unlock a phone being held as evidence in a crime, as the iPhone in question would erase all data after 10 failed unlocks. The matter was dropped after the bureau cracked the phone without Apple's assistance (it contained no information about the case).
Private messaging apps have also been used to gather sensitive information. In 2021, the FBI and the Australian government joined forces to lure in criminals with a supposed private messaging app, "ANOM." In reality, it was a way for the FBI to spy on active crimes and led to over 800 arrests.
Going after website owners - deepfakes, drugs, and rock-n-roll (MP3s)
The U.S. government has also intervened in websites and web hosting providers facilitating illegal activity. When a torrent search engine was seized in 2010, the owner told TorrentFreak, "My domain has been seized without any previous complaint or notice from any court!" In 2010 alone, the government shuttered 82 domains related to piracy. In 2015, Rocky P. Ouprasith was sentenced to 36 months in prison for running the "second-largest" music piracy website. More recently, hosts of AI deepfake pornography were hit with seizures, with 12 sites being taken offline.
Famously, the feds used the deep web's more illegal side, often dubbed the "dark web," to track down and arrest the owner of illegal drug-selling site, the Silk Road. Under the name "Dread Pirate Roberts," after the fantasy film "The Princess Bride," Ross Ulbricht utilized the deep web's encryption provided by the Tor network to mask its location. Ulbricht was caught in a San Francisco library, where two FBI agents distracted him as an arguing couple, and a third grabbed the laptop. Despite being sentenced to life in prison for masterminding the drug-selling site and other crimes uncovered from messages extracted from the laptop, Donald Trump pardoned Ulbricht in 2025.
There are plenty of other cases out there, and with artificial intelligence now readily available, it's likely the government will continue to step in — if orders are given, that is. The President recently stated that objectors to the rampant build-out of AI are "traitors."
articles.summary:
The U.S. government is increasingly challenging software features and digital tools, ranging from encrypted messaging and privacy-focused operating systems to websites facilitating illegal activities and cyberattacks.

### Key Points
- Federal authorities are currently litigating the use of GrapheneOS’s duress feature, which wipes device data during police seizures, citing statutes against the destruction of evidence.
- Proposed legislation like the STOP CSAM Act seeks to mandate backdoors in encrypted messaging platforms such as WhatsApp and Signal to monitor for illegal content.
- The FBI successfully utilized a fake messaging app, ANOM, to conduct a global sting operation in 2021, resulting in over 800 criminal arrests.
- High-profile government interventions include the 2013 Silk Road shutdown, the 2010 seizure of 82 piracy-related domains, and the 2016 legal battle with Apple over iPhone encryption.
- Security researchers have faced legal repercussions, including a 2019 wrongful arrest of two pentesters who were later awarded $600,000 in damages for a sanctioned Iowa judicial system breach.

### Why it Matters
These cases highlight a growing tension between individual digital privacy rights and federal law enforcement's investigative capabilities. As technology evolves, the government's efforts to regulate encryption and software functionality continue to shape the legal landscape for developers, activists, and everyday users.

- Enterprise AI spending has surged by 222% despite a 1,000% decrease in individual token costs, a phenomenon Peterson describes as an inversion of traditional efficiency.
- CloudZero data shows a 14-fold increase in generative AI spending over a five-month period, with 80% of costs attributed to overhead, R&D, and inefficient system loops.
- The "cost to build" has eclipsed the "cost to serve," as companies prioritize rapid AI adoption over tracking the business outcomes of their investments.
- Lack of standardized billing and "invisible" costs make it difficult for organizations to audit AI expenses, leading to potential "Denial-of-Wallet" security risks.
- Peterson predicts that by 2028, autonomous AI systems will handle the majority of code writing, deployment, and management, necessitating a shift toward unit-economic metrics.

### Why it Matters
The rapid, top-down adoption of AI is forcing a shift in corporate financial responsibility from engineering teams to the CFO’s office. Companies that fail to connect AI spending to measurable business outcomes risk significant financial instability and operational inefficiency as autonomous systems begin to dominate infrastructure.

articles.title: Cyberattack Targets French Supermarket Refrigerators, Forcing Mass Food Disposal
articles.author: Omar Gallaga
articles.content:
Hundreds of supermarkets in France were the subject of a coordinated hack early Monday morning that turned up the heat on fridges and freezers, causing food to spoil and, in some cases, fires to break out.
According to reports from AFP, three major grocery chains in the country — E. Leclerc, Intermarche and Cooperative U — reported that hackers forced connected fridges and freezers at hundreds of stores to go into defrost mode for several hours, raising their temperatures to 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit). Paris authorities told the news agency that other grocery chains were also hit.
While it’s unclear who is responsible for the attacks or the exact exploit chain used, the hackers targeted software on two Danfoss system controllers. The company told the industry publication Cooling Post that the affected systems, AK-SM800 and AK-SC355, were running outdated firmware. “We are working with affected customers to implement appropriate mitigation measures, including firmware updates where available, stronger network protections and removing direct internet exposure where applicable,” Danfoss told Cooling Post.
More from CNET
On a web page for its AK-SM800 controllers, Danfoss says the company “takes security seriously” and that “new measures are being implemented” to improve security.
A representative for Danfoss didn’t immediately return a request for comment.
The incidents are alarming for several reasons. In addition to proving yet again that network-connected devices, especially older ones, can be targets of attack, the French supermarket attack highlights vulnerabilities in global food supplies that can be quickly and dangerously exploited.
Dominique Schelcher, CEO of Cooperative U, said in a post on X that an investigation into the attack is underway. “Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented,” he posted (translated from French).
The ‘internet of things’ is being attacked
The attack on a French supermarket underscores the growing risk of attacks on operational technology and cold-chain infrastructure. Though the fridges and freezer units weren’t consumer smart fridges with app controls and touch screens, the controllers were connected to the internet to remotely manage defrost cycles, temperatures and alarms across many stores.
Companies may have many reasons for using these kinds of OT devices. They can log temperatures to ensure they’re meeting food safety standards, deploy firmware updates to prevent security incidents like this one and get alerts if a fridge or freezer is malfunctioning. Some devices like this also monitor inventory or even update prices for digital shelf displays.
But just as appliances from companies such as Samsung can be affected by a hack or even software glitches — like a recent incident in Korea that bricked some smart fridges — these industrial devices rely on imperfect software and internet connections, which expose them to the outside world.
Older IT and operational systems that are incorporated into connected systems may be especially difficult to defend, said Nathaniel Jones, senior vice president of global threat intelligence at Darktrace. “A cyber incident no longer affects only data or business systems; it can manipulate physical equipment and cause real-world damage.”
That damage can scale quickly if those systems are spread across many locations, all of which are exposed to the internet. “If it is connected, it can be targeted,” Jones said in a statement to CNET via email.
If that’s not scary enough, these are the same types of vulnerabilities that can make utilities such as power grids, water suppliers and even nuclear power plants vulnerable to attack.
articles.summary:
Hackers targeted hundreds of French supermarkets by exploiting outdated firmware in Danfoss controllers, forcing refrigeration units into defrost mode and causing significant food spoilage and equipment fires.

### Key Points
- Major grocery chains including E. Leclerc, Intermarche, and Cooperative U reported coordinated attacks on their refrigeration systems.
- Attackers remotely forced connected fridges and freezers to reach temperatures of 50 degrees Celsius (122 degrees Fahrenheit).
- The breach targeted Danfoss AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 system controllers that were running outdated, internet-exposed firmware.
- Danfoss is currently working with affected retailers to implement security patches and remove direct internet exposure for these industrial devices.
- French authorities and retail executives have launched investigations into the incident, citing the unprecedented nature of the threat to the national food supply.

### Why it Matters
This incident demonstrates how vulnerabilities in operational technology can lead to physical damage and significant disruptions to critical supply chains. It highlights the urgent need for businesses to secure internet-connected industrial equipment against cyber threats that can manipulate real-world infrastructure.

articles.title: XRP treasury Evernorth’s shares rise 5% at Nasdaq opening print
articles.author: Cointelegraph by Zoltan Vardai
articles.content:
XRP treasury Evernorth’s shares rise 5% at Nasdaq opening print
Evernorth’s share price rose by 5% as investors welcomed the Nasdaq debut of the first pure-play XRP digital asset treasury.
The newly listed shares of XRP-focused treasury company Evernorth Holdings (XRPN) jumped as much as 5% on their Monday Nasdaq stock exchange debut, according to Yahoo Finance data.
Earlier on Monday, the company named former Coinbase Asset Management Co-Chief Investment Officer Hugo Jeandesboz as its new chief investment officer. He will lead treasury strategy, including treasury allocation, liquidity management and the active management of Evernorth’s XRP holdings, according to a Monday announcement.
Evernorth deploys its XRP holdings to earn additional income through decentralized finance (DeFi) yield strategies.
On Oct. 2, shareholders of blank-check firm Armada Acquisition Corp. II approved the plan to combine the company with Evernorth. The company expects to hold about 473 million XRP, currently worth $657 million, which it said would make it the largest publicly traded XRP treasury company.
As for the XRP token, it was recently trading hands at $1.39 apiece with $1.48 billion worth traded in the past 24 hours, according to Coingecko data. At that price, XRP has a market cap of roughly $87.8 billion, making it the fifth-biggest cryptocurrency.
articles.summary:
Evernorth Holdings shares rose 5% during their Nasdaq debut on Monday, marking the launch of the first publicly traded company focused on managing a large-scale XRP digital treasury.

### Key Points
- Evernorth Holdings (XRPN) shares climbed 5% following the company's official listing on the Nasdaq stock exchange.
- The firm appointed former Coinbase executive Hugo Jeandesboz as chief investment officer to oversee treasury strategy and liquidity management.
- Evernorth plans to hold approximately 473 million XRP, valued at roughly $657 million, to become the largest publicly traded XRP treasury.
- The company generates additional income by deploying its XRP holdings through various decentralized finance (DeFi) yield strategies.
- The listing follows an October 2 shareholder approval to merge Evernorth with the blank-check firm Armada Acquisition Corp. II.

### Why it Matters
This listing provides institutional and retail investors with a regulated vehicle to gain exposure to XRP assets through traditional stock markets. By integrating DeFi yield strategies into a public treasury, the company represents a significant bridge between cryptocurrency holdings and conventional financial infrastructure.

articles.title: Homeowner comes home to discover his native pollinator garden has been damaged, discovers neighbor's trespassing $3,800 robotic mower is the culprit, repeated attempts to stop it crossing their shared boundary fail—homeowner takes more drastic measures
articles.author: Brad Dickson, Brad Dickson
articles.content:
The Events
This homeowner's neighbor purchased a $3,800 robotic mower that, despite its “smart” boundary settings, could not be contained. It repeatedly crossed into the homeowner's yard and damaged his prized native pollinator garden. The garden presented an investment of time and energy itself and was a point of pride for the homeowner, so they were crushed to see the cherished plants damaged.
Repeated attempts to resolve the situation and the originally apologetic neighbor's attempts to contain the robot via settings bore no fruit. So the homeowner went out and got $95 of metal landscaping edging and installed it along the boundary, well within his side of the property line.
You can probably see where this is going… The mower hit the metal edging, damaging the blades of the mower. Now the neighbor is demanding that the homeowner cover the cost of repairs and a replacement mower rental. The neighbor insists that the homeowner should have warned him, and another neighbor is arguing for a split of the costs just to keep the peace.
So who was in the wrong here? Is it the neighbor or the homeowner? Or do they both share in the blame?
Negotiating with neighbors
Disagreements in lifestyles, opinions, and needs are always going to create a need for negotiation. Reaching common ground and hashing things out is going to have to take place to avoid conflict. The problem is we have all grown so conflict-averse that we perceive the hard conversation as conflict instead of a necessity, so we avoid having the hard conversation in the first place, allowing our misgivings to fester and bad feelings to grow.
The boundary
I think the boundary isn't just between our properties… It's in our heads too.
It's really not that hard to go over to the fence and have a conversation about these things. Maybe flick one text message saying, “Hey, let's look at this at the fence.” And then go out and deal with the situation face-to-face
I stand by my feeling that a lot of the problems we have today stem from the abundance and “ease” of communication actually making things worse in the long run by adding uncertainty of meaning and interpretation to messages and back-and-forth exchanges, drawing out what could have been a quick face-to-face discussion.
But, in this particular instance, the homeowner did a great job of initially trying to set a boundary, adjust his neighbor's expectations, and fix the issue. But this didn't fix the problem, with the neighbor's attempts at recalibrating the machine.
Responsibilities of Out-of-Control Technology
How responsible are we for the impact of wayward technology that we control?
I mean that alone is something that we could probably talk about for hours, and it's a growing and ongoing source of debate.
Are you responsible for what you program a robot or AI software to do? Are you responsible if it does what you didn't think to tell it to do? Are you responsible for it malfunctioning?
I think of it like this: If you park your car on a hill, let's say it's a manual transmission, for the sake of the argument, even though they are rapidly going extinct. You set the parking brake, but it fails, and your car rolls down the hill and hits another vehicle. Are you responsible for the damage to that vehicle? Well, yeah, probably. You did everything right, but something in your possession and under your control did something unpredictable, so you're going to have to pay anyway.
The same is true for any technology system, automated, software, or mechanical. If it does something it shouldn't and damages something of someone else's… well, you're going to have to get your wallet out. Proverbially speaking.
But suppose your car rolls down the hill and strikes your neighbor's landscaping boulder that they have in front of their house. (I don't know, maybe they like boulders, ok?) You're not going to expect them to pay for the damage to your car… You're probably going to be paying for the damage to their boulder. The same is true here. Damage done by the robot should be paid for, but damage done to it when its “parking brake" fails and it goes somewhere it shouldn't, shouldn't.
Still, in keeping with the discussion and spirit of the original online community where this post was shared, the homeowner gave two options, allowing readers to select A or B as to how he should approach the situation.
So which should it be? A or B? Have a read of the original story below and some of the key responses. Then let us know your thoughts in the comments.
A or B: My neighbor's $3,800 robot mower kept crossing into my yard and damaged my garden. I added $95 of edging on my side, and now he wants me to pay for the repairs
Story source/Upper_Criticism3388
My neighbor and I share a straight property line between our front yards. Last spring, he bought a $3,800 robotic mower that uses a boundary wire. He was pretty excited about it and showed me how he could control it from an app.
Around the same time, I planted a small native pollinator garden on my side of the yard. It was just some native flowers and grasses that cost a few hundred dollars and took me a weekend to put together.
A few weeks later, I noticed his mower had crossed over the property line and damaged some of the plants. I sent him a photo, and he apologized and said he would adjust the boundary settings.
The same thing happened again a few times over the next month. Each time he said he would recalibrate it, but eventually the mower went further into my yard and damaged a larger section of the garden. My doorbell camera captured multiple instances of it crossing the property line.
I checked the property records to confirm the boundary and installed $95 of metal landscape edging a few inches inside my own yard to protect the garden. The edging was completely on my property, and there are no HOA rules against having it.
About a week later, my neighbor came over and said his mower had hit the edging and damaged the blades. He showed me a repair estimate and also asked me to cover the cost of renting a replacement mower while his was being repaired.
He believes I created a hazard near the boundary and should have warned him before installing it. I think his mower repeatedly entering my yard and damaging my plants is what caused the whole situation.
Another neighbor told me I should just split the cost to avoid creating bad bl**d over a lawn dispute.
A) I pay part of the repair cost and move the edging back to give his mower more clearance. A few hundred dollars is not worth creating a long-term feud with a neighbor.
B) His mower crossed onto my property multiple times and damaged my garden before I installed anything. I refuse to pay for the mower repairs and use the camera footage if he tries to make me responsible.
articles.summary:
A homeowner is facing a dispute with a neighbor after installing $95 of metal edging that damaged a $3,800 robotic mower that repeatedly trespassed onto his private property.

### Key Points
- A neighbor’s robotic mower repeatedly crossed property lines, damaging a native pollinator garden despite multiple attempts to recalibrate the device's boundary settings.
- The homeowner installed metal landscaping edging entirely within his own property line to protect his garden after documenting the mower's intrusions with a doorbell camera.
- The neighbor is now demanding the homeowner cover repair costs and a rental fee for the mower, claiming the edging created an unexpected hazard.
- The homeowner is currently weighing whether to pay for repairs to maintain peace or refuse payment based on the mower's history of trespassing.

### Why it Matters
This conflict highlights the growing legal and social complexities surrounding the accountability of automated consumer technology in residential settings. It underscores the necessity of clear communication and established liability standards when autonomous devices cause property damage or interact with neighboring landscapes.
